div.p: The uncle disowned. Children are to support their parents, or else be imprisoned. Two brothers were at odds with each other; one of them had a son. The uncle fell into poverty; though his father forbade it, the young man supported him; for this he was disowned, and said nothing. He was adopted by the uncle. The uncle, receiving an inheritance, became rich. The father began to be in want: with the uncle forbidding it, the young man supports him. He is disowned. He speaks against it.

He had now been brought to such a pass that he placed all his hope of last resort for support in that one house in which he kept a man both disowned and an enemy. "He himself," he says, "forbade me to be supported." Do you call the copying of another's fault innocence? Every prosperity is unstable and uncertain. Who would have believed, as Marius lay upon the rough sea-wall, that he had been a consul, or would be one again? What do you suppose the fortunate need not fear? What may the unfortunate not hope for? Not to send you off among more examples of fortune's instability, look at who is asked for support and who does the asking. I am no burdensome guest: I bring one old man. It is by this fault, father, that I have pleased you. The whole world would have perished, had mercy not put a limit to anger. Tossed between two fathers, the son of each, I am yet always disowned by the more fortunate one. Yet this, father, I call the gods to witness: I leave you a rich man. I will go round the doorways of strangers with you, father; I will show everyone both me, who gave support, and you, who refused it. I cannot be disowned for what I did under the compulsion of the law. What if you should forbid me to weep when I have seen a man in misery? Our feelings are not within our own power. Certain laws are unwritten, yet more certain than all that is written.

The other side. He has resolved to grow great out of the ill-will against me — a man who can boast of himself better than he can defend himself. My fear is a just one: that I may write an ungrateful man my heir, and leave behind me an enemy. Even if you do not hate the man who did me an injury, I hate the man who did you one. He ceases to be a son who has not only been disowned, but has been adopted by another as well. Hear how greatly I was in want: I begged of my brother. Who are you to pass judgement on the conduct of fathers? We do not refer our hatreds to you as arbitrator; we have the gods for judges.

Remarks made outside the controversia. Alfius Flavus, still in boy's dress, used to declaim controversiae in the school of Cestius. But his eloquence was always commended by something beyond eloquence; in the boy, his very age lent a charm to his talent.

The man to be adopted after three sons were disowned. A rich man disowned three sons; he asks a poor man for his only son in adoption. The poor man is willing to give him; when the son refuses to go, the father disowns him. The son speaks against it.

I never thought it would come about that either my father would hate his children or a rich man would covet them. Long I was in doubt: was the one trying out a friend, or the other a son? Are we then so poor, who have something rich men ask for? If he disowned them undeservedly, I hate a father who casts out so many innocent sons; if deservedly, I hate a house that makes so many guilty. I love poverty equally with my father; I am accustomed to both. Your house is not propped up by many children — though even so you ought not to have given me away; for he is safer against fortune who has something left after his loss. "I disown you," he says; it is plain where you come from. There is but one dispute between us: he thinks me worthy of a fortunate father, I think myself worthy of my own. "I want you to be rich," he says. O I deserve to be disowned, if I leave such a father behind! What you would have me seem I do not know: innocent? but I am disowned; guilty? but I am adopted. Not, as in other disownings, is it in my power not to be disowned: I shall lose my father if I am disowned, and lose him if I am not disowned. What difference is there whether I am cast out or transferred? Although a father is to be obeyed in all things, in this he is not to be obeyed — in that by which he ceases to be a father. It is hard to be without an only son; harder to be without the one whom another covets. The unknown herds of slaves do not delight their master, nor the sounding workhouses of a broad estate: I love my father for nothing. I must needs fear a house unlucky in its children. No fitter time for reconciliation can be found: the rich man is looking for sons.

The other side. Among the rest of poverty's drawbacks this too is great: that a son does not fear being disowned. Wealth raises a man to senatorial rank; wealth marks off the Roman knight from the commons; wealth promotes a man's rank in the camp; by wealth a juror is chosen in the forum. It is easier to praise poverty than to bear it. "If my sons are reformed," he says, "I shall have this one along with them; if they persist, I shall have him in their place."

Outside. Dry declaimers keep more faithfully to the colours they have proposed; for no sweetness of some epigram steals in upon them, no figure tempts them aside. So women who are plain are often chaste: it is not the will they lack, but the corrupter. Gallus Vibius was once a man of as great eloquence as he afterwards was of madness; and he is the only man I know to whom it happened that he came to madness not by chance but by deliberate choice; for while he imitated madmen, while he took frenzy for a charm of talent, what he was feigning he reduced to fact. Otho Junius the father published four books of colours, which our friend Gallio neatly calls the books of Antiphon: so much of dreams is there in them. Syriacus, against Maximus Stertinius, by whom he was being pressed hard, though he had been his companion, said: "For fifteen years I was in your service; tell me what wrong I have done. But this is your way: you call the end of servitude an injury."

The spendthrift blinded by his fellows. Let a blind man receive a thousand denarii from the public funds. Ten young men, when they had eaten up their goods, drew lots, so that the one whose name came out should, by their compact, be blinded and so receive a thousand denarii. The lot of one of them came out; he was blinded. He asks for the thousand denarii. They are refused.

These are the eyes you feared, husbands. O for a law to be repealed, if it blinds men! The commonwealth gives a thousand denarii to no one but him who receives it unwillingly. Say now, "have pity"; this you did not say when you were being blinded. The commonwealth consoles infirmity; it does not buy it. Their patrimonies consumed, they bring in their limbs. It is more useful to the commonwealth that one blind man be turned away than that nine more be made. He does not ask support of you alone, but first of many. I will support the man who is supported because of his infirmity; I will not support the man who is made infirm for the sake of support. So it falls out, when men spend the greater part of their lives in darkness, that at last they loathe the sun as superfluous.

The other side. He will give nothing to those nine: he will be in nobody's favour, if he cheats the men by whom he was blinded . . . The young man, encircled by those nine veteran spendthrifts, says: "Alone, I could not resist nine in agreement." It was all done by arrangement: one made the proposal, all approved it; one was chosen to draw the lots; his lot was put in to come out first. When he resisted, he was blinded. "If he was encircled," he says, "let him pursue the wrong, let him sue for violence, let him seek redress in kind." We shall see; the first thing is that he have something to live on.

The father dragged from the tombs by a spendthrift. A certain man who had lost three children, while he sat beside the tomb, was carried off by a dissolute young man into a neighbouring garden, had his hair shorn, and was compelled to take part in a banquet with his garments changed. Once let go, he sues for injuries.

Never are tears suppressed by command; nay, they are even provoked. There is no greater cause for weeping than not to be able to weep. He carried me off in such a state that I should be ashamed to come to a banquet, and let me go in such a state that I should be ashamed to return to the tomb. I suppose someone wonders that I come into the forum when I have just lost my children. But I have already been at a banquet. "How long," he says, "will you weep?" There is a certain pleasure for the wretched in their very ills, and all adverse fortune has its solace in lamentation. There you forbid me to weep, where you yourself would cruelly not weep. Since to weep is the most wretched thing, how unhappy am I, to whom not even this is allowed! I have seen the thirst of the drunken and the hunger of the vomiting. Who is this who demands the censorship of mourning over a weeping father? Flung into every outrage of gluttony and lust, to be marked by every censor, he composes precepts for the age: he knows how much a father ought to weep over three lost children — a man whom, if he lived, a father would weep. An old man, bereaved, unhappy, I take this one solace amid my miseries, that I cannot be more wretched. I see the ashes of my own in the tomb. It is a great solace to call again and again on the names of my children, that will not answer. Here I must live, lest I meet anyone, thinking of marriage, thinking of children, as a dire omen. He forces a man to weep who does not allow it . . . To linger at that banquet would be an injury even to a fortunate father.

The other side. I complained first of the inhumanity of those who were connected to him by kinship: is no one his friend, no one, I say, his kinsman? But they knew his frenzy better, I see. On a festal day my companions and friends were with me, one of whom said: "Why do we let this wretched man perish? No one sets a limit to weeping for himself; they are ashamed to leave off, they wish to be compelled." I would console you longer, were you not now able also to accuse me.

The cut noose. Let there be an action for recorded wrongdoing. A certain man, after a shipwreck, having lost three children and his wife in the burning of his house, hanged himself. One of the passers-by cut the noose for him. By the man he had freed he is made defendant for wrongdoing.

"I lost three children," he says. Would that I could have saved them too! Live; the turns of human fortune change: a proscribed man once proscribed others. The conquered flee, the proscribed lie hidden, the shipwrecked swim. "I lost," he says, "my wife, my children, my patrimony." Did you think you had received them on this condition, that you should never lose them? Fortune plays with her own gifts, and what she has given she takes away, what she has taken away she gives back; nor is it ever safer to make trial of her than when she has no room for injury. Gnaeus Pompeius, conquered in the line at Pharsalia, lived on. Do you think your own shipwreck greater? Crassus lived; and he had lost not private but public resources. Fortune has taken everything from you, but she has left you hope. Take away hope from men, and no conquered man will take up arms again, no one whose venture has failed will seek other gains, no shipwrecked man will live. Hope is the last solace of adversity. To live, you swam. I had pity, and I thought of nothing in your case beyond the danger: I did not attend to the fire, nor to your bereavement, or if I did attend to them, I remembered that you had lived after those things. He did not seem to me to have the mind to die: he had chosen a place where he could be interrupted.

The other side. I, master of so many estates, hang my noose from another man's tree. Of fortune I make no complaint: it permits me to die. "Now," he says, "die." It is an injury, that I who ought to die at my own pleasure should die at yours. I have lost wife, children, patrimony; fortune left me nothing but a noose, and this man not even a noose. I took up the instruments of death, solitude and a noose — the one fit for a dying man, the other for a wretched one. Whoever you are that come upon me, if a friend, weep; if you are an enemy, look on. Since I am accused by this man, pass a heavier sentence upon me than upon the defendant: that I may die, that he may not prevent it. Lest I should tell this tale, I wished to die. He cut short my remedy. If there is any faith to be had, I did not swim ashore, but was cast up. Now I feared nothing but to live. I am closing the destinies of my house, more wretched than any only in this — that I die last. For what life do you reserve me? To build? Look at the fire. To sail? Look at the shipwreck. To rear children? Look at the tomb. In so calamitous a house you were the more fortunate, my wife and children: to you it fell to die.

The bond with the disowned son. A brother gave his disowned brother a bond promising to give him half the inheritance if he did not speak against it. The disowned man kept silent. The other is disowned by the father.

He has as much debt as he could not pay while his father lives. Do you wish to know what your credit is worth? Not even your brother trusted you without a bond. The one I delay in his hope, the other in his good faith. I am alive, and already my patrimony has been divided. Unless you help me, even the man who kept silent will defeat me. I do not conceal that today I am disowning two. Bring out the bond, the compact of parricides and the pact of unholy hope, the bond impious in the giver, base in the receiver, dangerous to the father.

The other side. In every fortune, brother, I will join myself to you as your companion: if there is soldiering to do, we will soldier together; if travel abroad, together we will wander through cities; if I beg my daily alms, even that I will share with you. I did not wish my father's fresh anger to be stirred up; I preferred that, by keeping silent, he should overcome our father. I will be heir of my own portion, guardian of yours. And because in the greatest matters each man trusts himself best, I give the bond; do you take care to seem to receive that portion rather from your father than from your brother. This thing which we were doing honourably and dutifully, we did so openly that our father knew it. For what did I fear? That, if my father learned of it, he would take it ill that his son is no greedy man, that his brother is dutiful? So may it fall to me that my father be reconciled to us both.

The man released by his son the pirate chief. A certain man brought a stepmother in over his two sons. He condemned one of them at home for parricide; he handed him over to his brother for punishment. The brother put him on a ship stripped of its tackle. Carried to the pirates, the young man became a pirate chief, captured his father as he travelled, and let him go. On his return the father disowns his son.

Bewildered by so great a storm, I could discern nothing, nor did I well remember whether my father or my stepmother had laid such a service upon me, whether he had meant it to be a service or a punishment, the avenging of parricide or a parricide. You bid me sew my brother into a sack? I cannot. Do you not forgive me? Or do you not believe me? I maintain that not even you could do it. No companion of his shipwreck was found; all the tackle was cut away, no support for hope. Am I to be excused to my father or to my brother? "This gift of your filial love I shall bear to the world below — that it was permitted me, through my brother, to die otherwise than as a parricide." "Your brother lives," he says. I do not believe it. "He saved me," he says. You have made me believe it. In a house in which a parricide was so easily believed, I could not kill my brother, nor my brother our father. Description of the storm: lightnings flashed from thick clouds on every side, and dread tempests had hidden the day; the sea had swollen, dreadful even to sound ships. "You have," I said, "brother, if you are innocent, a ship; if guilty, a sack." I could not commit parricide — how easily we all go astray — and thought it committed. "Brother," he said, "you will be the first in the house to commit parricide." There lay on the shore the ship that, even whole, had carried him unhappily. I will believe him a parricide, if he gave you back his own ship as you set out. Suddenly the blade slipped from my hand together with my courage, and by some bewilderment darkness was poured over my dazed eyes. I understood how hard it was to commit a parricide, even one a father had commanded. So may Fortune help me — she who alone looks upon the wretched in our house. My father set out on a calm sea, with a favourable journey, in a sound ship. What is this? The condemned man sailed more happily than the man who had condemned him. Do you think he learned innocence among the pirates, or that he did not lose it even among the pirates? You would have perished, father, had you not fallen in with a parricide. The very torn sails had filled out, and the shipwrecked vessel had outrun equipped fleets. You would know that the man was sailing who was to save his father. There was a ship — nay, there had been one. O cruel and stubborn stepmother! She rages no less; the seas are now at rest, the pirates show mercy, the angry spare. I have come to you to prove myself a parricide. Nature has opened many roads to death, and by many paths the fates run their course. O seas juster than verdicts! O storms milder than a father! Do you not think him merciful, who gave the man he had condemned to his brother for punishment? Lucullus's centurion could not kill Mithridates — Mithridates, good gods, how unquestionable a parricide! Rejoice, father, neither of your sons committed parricide. Tell, father, how he let you go, having been so let go himself. "He is guilty," you say; but to me he is a brother. The laws of nature are sacred even among pirates. "You should have said," he says, "that you could not." So did you not know it? It was not lawful, I ought not, I could not.

The other side. Deny now that he was a parricide, when you know he is a pirate. He let me go for his own defence, so that, because he had not killed me, he might seem not even to have wished it before. And who, moreover, is more wretched than I alone? I owe my life to a parricide.

Outside. A great band of the newer rhetoricians went over to this side, holding that something ought to be said against the stepmother; and there were those too who would not say it openly, but by hint and figures; which Passienus did not approve, asserting that to defame a stepmother is less modest or tolerable than to accuse her. Some had only their openings in their own power; afterwards they were carried away by impulse. It is more excusable to fall into a bad colour than to cross into it. Hispanus, using a harsh colour, said that he had chosen this kind of punishment as the graver: which colour displeased the prudent; for what hope of acquittal has a man, if he neither obeyed nor spared?

The bereaved sacrilegious woman after the noose. Let the magistrate exact punishment of a woman who has confessed. A certain woman, having lost her husband along with two of her children, hanged herself. A third son cut the noose for her. When a sacrilege had been committed and the sacrilegious person was being sought, she told the magistrate that she had committed the sacrilege. The magistrate wishes to exact punishment of her as of one who has confessed; her son speaks against it.

I do in the forum, judges, what I did at home: I keep my mother from dying. "How did you do it?" he says. "In what place did you hide what you had carried off?" She faltered, and knew nothing of sacrilege but its penalty. Having lost two children, she seemed to herself sacrilegious because she lived. I have come, not to plead beside her, but to save her. Others entreat for defendants; I shall entreat for a defendant. The accuser has no witness except on my benches. There is no confession except when the accuser digs out the truth, the defendant denies, the torturer forces it out. It is said that a certain woman, on seeing her son beyond hope, expired. If great joy drives mothers to death, what does great grief do? Mother, you have no slight solace: you see that even the gods lose something. The wretched worship the gods more than the fortunate. The woman did not commit the sacrilege; the old woman did not; the bereaved did not; she who is being guarded did not; she who confesses did not. "Angry at the gods," he says, "she could commit sacrilege." The spirit is broken in the calamitous, and unhappiness itself condemns itself; and the human condition has even this for its worst, that fortune makes those it has made wretched superstitious too. The gods are worshipped more carefully by the angry. Who, then, did it? How can I know, who was guarding my mother? I plead the cause of the laws, that the executioner with which they threaten the sacrilegious they may not bring against the calamitous. She worshipped the gods so as to fear so much for so many.

The other side. Confession is the voice of a guilty conscience. Confession is the word of one compelled, and of one acknowledging what she did. The voice of all was: "The sacrilege cannot lie hidden; whoever it is, he will not himself make a good end, nor any of his own; and if there be no accuser, he will tell of it himself." Roused, she came forward, as though the gods themselves were pursuing her; "I did it," she said. Let us men exact punishment even now of the woman of whom the gods long ago began to exact it. By the majesty of the violated divinities she was driven both to wish to die, and to deserve it, and not to be able. The noose was cut for her. Did you think, sacrilegious woman, that you could die in secret? She did everything to keep silent, who, that she might not confess, even wished to die. If you seek the crime, the sacrilege was committed; if the sacrilegious one, she confesses. Do you seek the cause of the deed? If before she lost her children, greed; if after she lost them, anger.

Cimon ungrateful to Callias. Whoever catches an adulterer with the adulteress, provided he kill both, shall be free of guilt. Let there be an action for ingratitude. Miltiades, condemned for embezzlement, died bound in prison. His son Cimon, to bury him, gave himself as a substitute for his father's body. Callias, a rich man of base birth, ransomed him from the commonwealth and paid the money, and gave him his daughter in marriage. Cimon, catching his wife in adultery, killed her, though her father pleaded for her. He is accused of ingratitude.

To me, adultery is a prison. Shall I throw away the sword handed me by the law for the avenging of chastity? You lost your money, Callias, if you freed such hands. A high-born spirit cannot endure insult. This is the difference between the fortune of the father and the son: that for him prison was the end of his calamities, for me the beginning. The one whole estate of Miltiades that was found was his son Cimon. Cimon ransomed is the good fortune of his ransomer. I will return the favour when you have asked for one as honourable as the one you gave. Shall I let adulterers go? What else would I do, if I still had my hands bound? What? Do you think it a punishment to be bound for Miltiades? We each, while we gave a great benefit, received one: I, in that I ransomed Miltiades; you, in that you ransomed Cimon. I thought it most disgraceful that both adulterers and Cimon should be let go by the same man. I am the man who does not cease to return thanks even to the dead: so may it fall to me to have true children — and how great that is, Miltiades found by experience. Callias deserved to have begotten such a man as he ransomed. Say now, "I freed you from prison," that I may answer, "I gave myself to prison." It will never come about that I think it better done that I was ransomed by Callias than that I was bound for Miltiades. I thought myself ransomed by you: you bought me for your daughter. I married Callias's daughter: this wrong, father-in-law, I did to you, while I am unwilling to be ungrateful. I cannot be condemned for what I did by law. It is a benefit which is wholly bestowed for the sake of the man on whom it is conferred; where a man hopes for or prepares something out of it, it is not a benefit but a calculation. I freed you from the utmost dishonour; you received the benefit unwillingly. You ransomed me, and that without my asking. Set here the Verginii, and all who have either shut up or killed their violated daughters.

The other side. I gave two benefits: I both ransomed him and gave him my daughter in his need. I charge you with this, that you suffered your wife to become an adulteress, that you did not guard her, that you delayed until her father came up as a spectator of his own calamity. I had not waited until I was asked. You took it ill that Callias was called your father-in-law. You not only suffered the girl's character to slip into vices, but yourself drove it; having found the occasion, you did not let it slip.

Outside. The colour pleased Gallio and Latro and Montanus, that nothing should be said insultingly against Callias, against the ransomer, against the father-in-law, against the unhappy man. Many things said by the Greeks the Roman orators, historians, and poets did not steal, but challenged. There is a saying of Thucydides: "For prosperity is apt to cover over and shadow the faults of each." Of Sallust: "Prosperity is wonderfully a screen for vices." Since the chief virtue in Thucydides is brevity, in this Sallust outdid him, and felled him in his own camp. For in the Greek saying, brief as it is, you have what you may take away with the sense unharmed: remove either "cover over," or "shadow," or "of each," the sense will stand, even if not equally trim, yet equally whole. But from Sallust's saying nothing can be taken away without loss of sense. Titus Livius, however, was so unfair to Sallust that he charged this very saying against him as both translated and as corrupted in the translating: and he does it not from love of Thucydides, that he should prefer him, but he praises one he does not fear, and thinks Sallust can be more easily conquered by himself if he is first conquered by Thucydides.

The poor man's son following the rich man in mourning. Let there be an action for injury. A certain man who had a son and a rich enemy was found killed and unstripped. The young man, in mourning dress, began to follow the rich man. The rich man brought him to court and demanded that, if he suspected anything, he should bring the charge. The young man said: "I will accuse you when I can." The rich man, seeking offices, was rejected; he accuses the poor man's son of injury. The son speaks against it.

I thank the rich man, that he is now content to make defendants of those he hates. "You shall not walk," he says, "by the same road, you shall not tread in my footsteps, you shall not offer to my delicate eyes a mourning garment, you shall not weep against my will, you shall not keep silent." We would have perished, had this man been a magistrate. That I wore mourning is from grief; that I wept, from filial love; that I did not accuse, from fear; that he was rejected, that is your doing. While my father lived, he never sought offices. My own fault follows me: I keep silent. Would that my father too had had this fault! When have we ever not been in mourning before you? "Accuse," he says, "poor man, the rich." I am not even allowed to walk at my own discretion. "Accuse," he says, "carry the charge through, plead it out." Who can accuse a man who speaks so? "Why," he says, "do you follow me?" Have the poor, then, one road and the rich another? Whatever slayer rushed upon him, like a rich man, despised the spoils. When my father was killed — for I fear that someone may think himself injured if I say "killed." "You are in mourning," he says, "you weep." What else can I do, the son of a murdered poor man? What would he have done to an accuser, who pursues a man who keeps silent? "Why," he says, "do you follow me?" That you may someday pity me, that you may cease to pursue an afflicted house. I have for accuser a man who wonders that he is not a defendant. "Why do you not bring the action?" Because you so little fear it that you compel it. I am in mourning. Is what is permitted a defendant not permitted a mourner? Or shall I not even mourn the man whom I cannot avenge? There was no booty in him that a footpad might desire; there was the highest virtue, an innocence stubborn against the disdain of riches: these were the spoils sought by an enemy. Who contrived the murder, I cannot know; what cannot be concealed, I do know — who wished for it. Both you are a rich enemy, and he was found unstripped: there is no reason why I should accuse, but there is reason why I should suspect.
The other side. That you may know you are stirring up ill-will against me: when I had said, "accuse me," you did not refuse, but answered: "I will accuse you when I can."

The priestess who had been a prostitute. Let a priestess be chaste, born of the chaste, pure, born of the pure. A certain virgin, captured by pirates, was put up for sale; she was bought by a pimp and made a prostitute. She would entreat those who came to her for an alms. A soldier who had come to her, when he could not be entreated and tried to wrestle with her and use force, she killed. She was accused, acquitted, and sent back to her own people. She seeks a priesthood. There is opposition.

Your priestess would still be living in the brothel, had she not killed a man. What use to me is a priestess whose chastity hangs by a thread? This alone was wanting — that the temples should receive women whom either the prison or the brothel has cast out. I would call you unworthy of the priesthood even if you had merely passed through a brothel. "Fortune compelled me to suffer it, and all should pity me." But we do not make our priestesses out of objects of pity, nor is the highest honour among us the consolation of the worst of evils. So well was she guarded at home that she could be carried off; so dear was she to her own people that, once carried off, she was not ransomed; the pirates spared their captive only to sell her to a pimp; the pimp bought her only to prostitute her; she entreated those who came to her only until there was need of the sword. I am moved by my regard for all our virgins, if in the whole city no one could be found more chaste than a prostitute nor more pure than a killer. No woman is chaste enough about whom there is an inquiry. "I entreated them all," she says. If anyone doubted whether she was a prostitute, let him hear how seductive she is. Let us suppose three women seek the priesthood: one who was taken captive, another who has prostituted herself, a third who has killed a man — to all I say no.

The other side. The gods willed that there should be a marvel: liberty in a captive, modesty in a prostitute, innocence in one who has killed. Tell it freely, all of you, that men came to her as to a prostitute — so long as they left her as from a priestess. How chaste she is, the soldier showed; how innocent, the judge; how favoured of heaven, her return. Amid so many dangers the gods would not have preserved her, had they not meant to preserve her for themselves. The people brought to the saving of her chastity all that it had brought to the violating of it. Let her render to the gods the chastity she owes them.
Outside. One must keep far away from all that is obscene in words and in thoughts. Some things it is better to leave unsaid, to the detriment of one's case, than to say, to the detriment of decency.

The oath of husband and wife. A husband and wife swore that, if anything happened to one of them, the other would die. The husband went abroad; he sent a messenger to his wife to say that he had died. The wife threw herself down. Revived, she is ordered by her father to leave her husband; she will not. She is disowned. She speaks against it.

Immortal gods, with what wisdom you owe and you rule the human race: you brought it about that this should be not a danger to one who loved, but a test. Does my father-in-law wish to part those whom not even death will part? "I will die," she says; "I have both cause and example: some women have flung themselves into the burning pyres of their husbands, some have bought their husbands' safety with their own lives. By a brief anxiety this girl is counted, alive, among these." There were constant rivalries: "I cannot live without you" — "no, rather, I cannot live without you"; and as such contests usually end, we swore an oath. This without doubt was the mind of those who swore: that they should not be parted in life, since they took precaution even for this — that they should not be divided by death.

The other side. "I cannot," she says, "leave my husband." Can she not do anything, who can die? She had hardly sent the message of a false death when she received the message of a true one. You can bear to be without your husband; you have borne his journey abroad. You have already been freed of your oath by the latest chance.

Outside. Ovid Naso declaimed this controversia in the school of Arellius Fuscus, his teacher; for he was an admirer of Latro. Latro in a certain preface had said: "Do you not see how a torch, when unmoved, grows dull, and recovers its fire when shaken? Leisure softens men; iron contracts rust through lying idle." Naso said: "I myself have seen flames grow when the torch was shaken, and again die when no one stirred them." This man too said: "The whole labour lies in this — that you grant a wife to love her husband and a husband to love his wife. Then you must needs permit them to swear, if you have permitted them to love." By the same man: "You know few of my faults, father: we have quarrelled at times, and have fallen, and — what perhaps you do not think — we have sworn falsely." Asked once by his friends to strike out three lines, he in turn asked that three be excepted, over which they should have no power. They had written in secret the lines they wanted struck out, he the ones he wanted kept safe: in both sets of tablets the same lines were found, of which, the story goes, the first was — Albinovanus Pedo had been among the arbiters — "the half-bull man and the half-man bull"; the second: "and the chill North Wind and the unchill South." From which it appears that this man of the highest talent lacked not judgement to restrain the licence of his verses, but the will. He used to say that a face was sometimes more becoming for having some mole upon it.
The parricide acquitted by an even vote. A certain man accused his son of parricide. When the son was acquitted by an even vote, he disowns him.

What I now ask is less; I do not seek that you avenge me against a parricide, but that you separate me from him. I do not accuse the parricide, I flee from him. When will this man spare an accuser, who did not spare a father? Is there, then, nothing between the will and the sack? Not an acquitted parricide, but a doubtful one: to be acquitted you need many votes; to be condemned, one. They did not acquit the defendant, but spared the age. Do you wonder at mercy in a city in which the law grants acquittal even on equal tablets? Do you ask by how many you are disapproved? If I add one, you are a parricide. You owe your acquittal to the law, not to your innocence. "I was acquitted," he says. I do not disown you for parricide, but for other vices that made you so credible a parricide.
The other side. The young man's colour is plain: that he should say he was overborne by his father's authority.
The blinded Metellus. Let a priest be whole. The pontifex Metellus, when the temple of Vesta was burning, lost his eyes while snatching the Palladium. The priesthood is refused him.

Mother Vesta, perhaps you would have no priest, had you not had Metellus. I plead the cause of the holy rites, not of Metellus: it concerns them more that Metellus not lose the priesthood, than it concerns Metellus. Metellus was not yet so great when we gave him the priesthood. The anxious city hung in suspense; two things were in peril than which the people had nothing more precious, the sacred objects and Metellus. O the man who must be made priest, were he not so already! The law refers wholeness to the mind, not to the body. The law willed this to be assessed then, when a man sought the priesthood, not when he held it. You have, Vesta, a double merit of your pontifex: he saved the sacred things and did not see them.
Outside. Pollio: if he had been made blind before this, he would not have lifted them; if he was made blind afterwards, he saw.

The other side. A priest not whole of body is a thing to be avoided, as of ill omen. This is marked even in victims; how much more in priests? After the priesthood, infirmity is the more to be watched; for not without the anger of the gods is a priest made infirm. It is plain that the gods are not propitious to a priest whom they do not save even when he saves.

Outside. This colour Gallio did not approve, asserting, with the highest honour to Metellus, that the case must be argued against Metellus in such a way that he too be compelled, along with the judges, to consult the duty of the pontiffs.

The son-in-law of a rich enemy. A poor man who had a son, and a rich enemy who had a daughter, set out abroad. There was a rumour of his death. The son made peace with the rich man and married his daughter. The father, on his return, compels him to repudiate his wife; when he refuses, he disowns him.

No one easily believes anything which, if believed, must be grieved over. I, for a long time, did not believe the report of your marriage. Deserter of your father, client of his enemy, slave of your wife, you did not weep for your father, you did not seek for him; thus you pleased his enemy. "There had been a rumour," he says, "that you had died." I wondered if you could have had such a wife while your father lived. Do you not ask where I perished? My death ought to be suspect to you: I have an enemy. Who else could have set this report abroad but the man who, while I lived, could not give his daughter in marriage? Do you not fear that, in the very midst of your wedding, your father's bones may be brought back? So many slaves attend me, so many freedmen, so many clients, that whatever one of them says becomes a rumour. Fabricius would not take gold from Pyrrhus; he was richer in spirit than the other in his kingdom. I escaped several ambushes on my journey, and the rich man believed that done which he had ordered to be done.

The other side. Hatred of riches is an empty kind of glory. Enmities ought to be mortal. Scipio was Gracchus's enemy, and yet afterwards his father-in-law. Through whose fault the enmity was contracted is plain: he loves your son, you do not love even your own.

Outside. Senianus said a very foolish thing: "The rich man always despised me, never held me as other than dead." That I too may say something like Senianus, after this epigram I always held Senianus as dead.

The exiled father barred by the country-house. Let it not be lawful to help an exile with shelter and food. Let one condemned for unintentional homicide be exiled for five years. A certain man, who had a son and a daughter, condemned for unintentional homicide, set out into exile and used to come to an estate that bordered on his own. The son learned of this and beat the overseer; the overseer shut the father out. He began to go to his daughter. She, accused of having received an exile, was acquitted with her brother as advocate. After five years the father disowns the son.

The accuser made me an exile from my city, the son from my own people too. I found my daughter more honourable, in that she was accused; my slave more thrifty, in that he was beaten. You deserved ill of your father, whom you shut out; of your sister, whom you harmed by a precedent; of the judges, whom you feared in so good a cause. Either you did wrong, or your sister. My own son taught me, in that I do not receive him. "My sister," he says, "was acquitted with me as advocate." So you would not receive your father, when you could plead this cause so well? When the woman who had received him was acquitted, the man who had driven him out was condemned. My daughter judged me her father, my slaves their master; to my son alone I was an exile. Forgive me, most faithful of little slaves, I unwittingly harmed you too. How good do you think that cause was, which was not condemned even with you as advocate? If I can die with you as my heir, I am worthy to leave you even this slave. To another he is an exile, to you he is a father. No law commands a crime. At least she who did it was acquitted. The law holds the man who helped an exile, not the one who suffers him to be helped. Be ignorant, pretend not to see: the law bids you be innocent, not inquisitive. If you were doing it for my sake, you would have warned me, you would have barred the slave, you would not have beaten him.

The other side. I could not act when the law forbade. She was accused and acquitted, because she seemed a poor woman who did not know the laws. I feared not for myself but for you: the matter had come to men's knowledge; you were being hunted; I feared you would be killed. Do you wish to know it was known? My sister was accused. I chose to beat a most thrifty slave rather than to lose the best of fathers.

Popilius the slayer of Cicero. Let there be an action concerning character. Cicero defended Popilius, charged with parricide; he was acquitted. Sent by Antony, he killed the proscribed Tullius; he carried his head back to Antony. He is accused concerning his character.

Popilius killed Cicero. Do you now believe that this man killed his father? Meaning to kill Cicero, he should have begun with his father. "Antony ordered it," he says. Are you not ashamed, Popilius? Your commander believed you capable of committing parricide. He cut off the head, lopped off the hand. There is less crime in him that he killed Cicero. Good gods! I call the killing of Cicero a bad character. This alone is fortunate, that you killed your father before Cicero. More easily did Cicero move a judge for a parricide than himself for his client. To you, advocates, this precedent looks: Popilius hates none more than those to whom he owes most. He cut off the neck. Spare now, Popilius: Antony bade you do nothing but kill. Be ashamed, Popilius: your accuser lives. Antony would not have believed Popilius would do it, had he not remembered that he had committed parricide. The spirits of the dead, of old Popilius, and his father's unavenged shade pursue you, Cicero, that you may know him a parricide whom you denied to be one. The Minturnaean marsh did not swallow the exiled Marius; the Cimbrian saw him giving commands even in captivity. Gnaeus Pompeius, tamer of lands and sea, gladly professed himself the client of Hortensius; and Hortensius had defended Pompey's goods, not Pompey. So you, Popilius, if Antony had ordered it, would have killed even your father?

The other side. If you call those times into question, you speak not of a man's character, but of the commonwealth's. Do you wonder if at that time it was necessary for Popilius to kill, when it was necessary for Cicero to die? Cicero's proscription was to be killed, mine was to kill: my commander ordered it, my conqueror ordered it; could I refuse anything to the man to whom the commonwealth could refuse nothing?
Outside. Few of the historians have related that Popilius was the slayer of Cicero, and these too not that he was defended by Cicero on a charge of parricide, but in a private suit.

Phidias with his hands cut off. Let a sacrilegious man's hands be cut off. The Eleans received Phidias from the Athenians, to make for them the Olympian Jupiter, a compact being made that they should give back either Phidias or a hundred talents. When the Jupiter was finished, the Eleans said that Phidias had stolen the gold, and cut off his hands as a sacrilegious man, and give him back mutilated to the Athenians. The Athenians demand the hundred talents. The Eleans speak against it.

I can no longer lend you Phidias. That majesty can be expressed only when the mind has foreseen the work and the hands have drawn it. He made Jupiter for himself before he made him for the work. You are the sacrilegious ones, who cut off consecrated hands. The first blood the god saw was his own craftsman's. I call to witness Jupiter, now Phidias's own god. Art sustains others in misery; you it has made most miserable. The compact had been made by the hands that made Phidias what he was. Do you think we shall take back Phidias without that without which you would not have received him? We lent one who could make gods; we have taken back one who cannot even worship them. Are you not ashamed to owe a Jupiter to a sacrilegious man? The man survives, but the craftsman has perished. You give us back the penalty of Phidias, not Phidias. Hands that were wont to make gods now cannot even beg of men. He made such a Jupiter that the Eleans wished this to be his last work. We lent hands, we demand hands back. The Elean is witness, the Elean accuser, the Elean judge, the Athenian only defendant. I invoke the gods, both those whom Phidias made and those he could have made. We have taken back Phidias — I confess it, if we can lend him.

The other side. We had gold once sacred, we had ivory; for the sacred material we sought a craftsman. We had indeed arranged that Phidias should make images for other temples too, but it was not so necessary to adorn the gods as to avenge them.

Flamininus punishing a defendant at dinner. Let there be an action for treason. The praetor Flamininus, at dinner, being asked by a prostitute, who said she had never seen a man beheaded, killed one of the condemned. He is accused of treason.

Do I charge him with luxury, play-acting, jests? Or do you do nothing else at a banquet but kill? For a single kiss, perhaps, he made a gift of a homicide. About to dine, the executioners wash their hands. I do not inquire into the whole year; I am content with one night. It is easier that a man who has given much to a prostitute should deny a homicide, than that a man who has given a homicide should deny anything. If you had wished a slave to be flogged, you would have taken him out of the banquet. A table touched with human blood, axes drawn in the dining-room: who believes that a prostitute longed for these things, or that a praetor did them? The rods are brought out, and before the table and the gods a victim of cruelty is butchered. Wretched me, you made a plaything of the terror of the Roman empire. Let him fall to the law rather than to a harlot. Rise up, you Bruti, Horatii, Decii, and all the other glories of the empire: with your fasces, with your axes, now obscene girls make sport. In that which is done under the cover of the public majesty, whatever wrong is committed must be avenged by an action for treason. The lictor, about to strike, looks to the praetor, the praetor to the prostitute.

The other side. If an envoy brings false instructions, they are heard as though the Roman people had given them; if a general strikes a treaty, the Roman people seems to have struck it and is bound by the treaty: yet now nothing has been taken from the strength of the people nor from its repute. But men judge the rest from you. Both before him there were others by whom they could be judged. No one ascribes the vices of individuals to cities. They charge that a condemned man perished to please a prostitute, and they demand that a praetor perish for a condemned man. All the lust is within the prostitute, all the cruelty within the prison. The Roman people has borne many things in its commanders: in Manlius the want of self-control, by whom even his own son and a victor was killed; in Sulla cruelty; in Lucullus luxury; in many greed. I did not think it pertinent where or when a man should perish who deserved to perish. Who was killed? A condemned man. Where? In the praetorium. At what time? Is there then a time at which a guilty man ought not to perish?

Outside. There are certain controversiae in which the deed can be defended but cannot be excused. We do not hope that the judge will approve of Flamininus, but that he will acquit him; and so we ought to plead as for a deed not corrected, but not criminal. Titus Livius, of orators who hunt after antique and mean words and think the obscurity of an orator to be severity: "Yet in these, even if there is less madness, there is less hope. Those who swell, who labour under abundance, have more frenzy, but more body too; it is always easier to bring to soundness what can be cured by taking away; he cannot be helped who at once both raves and is wanting." Murredius spoke a tetracolon: "The forum was a slave to the bedchamber, the praetor to the prostitute, the prison to the banquet, the day to the night." The last clause was spoken without sense, that the sense might be filled out; for what sense has "the day was a slave to the night"? I have related this saying for this reason, that both in tricola and in all sayings of this kind we take care that the number be complete, and do not take care that the sense be. But I set out all kinds of corrupt sayings on purpose, because we are more easily taught by example both what is to be imitated and what avoided.

The brave man not yielding to his brave father. Let there be a reward for a brave man; if there are several, let them contend by a trial. A father and son did a brave deed. The father asked his son to yield to him; the son refused. They contended by a trial; the son defeated his father. With his reward he sets up statues for his father. He is disowned.

What issue of this trial to wish for I do not know, since my crime is to have won. I have the judgement of my country, I have lost that of my father. I saw my father in the line, I fought after his example. Does he call it a trial, that father and son brought our spoils together? I won, not as a son against a father, but as a young man against an old one. I won, but all congratulated my father. I thought of Horatius pushing back the Etruscan lines with his own body; I thought of Decius, who did not yield even to his own father. I was fighting not only for my general, but for my father too. I am greedy of glory: if this is a fault, it is a paternal one. Be ashamed, father, if your son, who is to be disowned, defeated you. I have the reward; you have both the reward and a brave man. Our virtues would have passed by in silence; they were made illustrious when they were compared. They judged not what was, but what they believed you preferred. The honour reached us both: one has the reward, the other received it.

The other side. I do not wish to dwell with my adversary. The same lodging does not hold a conquered man and a brave one. "I have set up statues," he says, "for you." Nay, that I might never be able to forget that I was conquered, you have cut my disgrace in bronze.

The unchaste woman from the rock. Let an unchaste woman be cast down from the rock. A woman condemned for unchastity, before she was cast down, called upon Vesta; cast down, she lived. She is demanded back for punishment.

This alone was wanting — that she should be more virtuous on the rock than she had been in the shrine. Can there be any doubt that she must be cast down again and again, until the very thing is brought about for which she was cast down? She thinks the misfortune of her perishing serves as her defence. What am I to pray for, troublesome woman, except that you not perish even when twice cast down? Shall I set out with whom, or when, she committed her defilement? Because I proved these things, you condemned her. Do you not think the law took precaution that she should perish, when it took precaution as to how she should perish? You judge ill of the gods, if they come to their priestess's aid so late. Did the gods then prefer to acquit a condemned woman rather than a priestess?

The other side. Condemned, she was cast down; acquitted, she came down. You would think the girl was not flung down but lowered. The law would not have deferred a priestess all the way to the rock, had it not been awaiting the verdict of the gods. The height of the cliff was dreadful even to those who looked down from it without danger.

The ravisher who does not win over the father. Let a ravisher, unless within thirty days he has won over both his own father and the father of the ravished woman, perish. A ravisher won over the ravished woman's father; he does not win over his own. He prosecutes him for madness.

Why do you tremble, old age? Why, tongue, do you falter? Why have you gone numb, my eyes? It is not yet the thirtieth day. Not even with a sadder face did he take his daughter's chastity stormed away from her. He was won over too quickly. Not to trace all his vices back to boyhood: he ravished a virgin; he prosecutes his father — all this within thirty days. Do you think I shall promise to an accuser what I refused to a son? Do you wonder that a father hesitates? The law itself hesitates between death and marriage. He has always believed that everything was permitted him; he has never asked anything of me. "He pardoned the man," you say. So was anyone asked before me? I am mad, you see; doubtless I live disgracefully, I know nothing of the law, I do not count your days. "You are mad," you say. Can anyone pardon a man who asks like this? "I will deliberate with my friends, I will deliberate with my kinsmen." Wretched me, how nearly I promised! Wretched me, that I have only thirty days to be angry! Why do you wonder if you won over the other man more quickly? It is easier to forgive an injury than a crime. Come forward into the midst, old man, by whose mercy I am made cruel. "Now," he says, "the time is short — and have you leisure to prosecute?" Is this how a man wins another over? Is this how he pleads? It is plain that now for the first time you are asking. For what have I done like a madman? I have not been won over. The time has not yet passed; even now I can be won over. How unfair it is that I am not yet guilty and already a defendant!

The other side. Wretched me, father! Nothing has been taken from your anger, much from the time. I am more unfortunate than if I had won over neither. If you mean to save your son, there has already been time; if to kill him, there is time now. The man who was more feared was asked first.

The man to be disowned who adopted his disowned brother. Let a father divide the patrimony with a son in his thirtieth year. A certain man had a thrifty son and a dissolute one. He disowned the dissolute one. The thrifty one set out abroad; he was captured by pirates; he wrote to his father about his ransom. While the father held back, the dissolute son forestalled him and ransomed his brother. The thrifty son returned; he adopted his brother. He is disowned.

There is no reason for anyone to praise me: my brother first set between us the example of family devotion; together he sailed, together he ran the risk, together he traversed every land, leaving me only at our father's house. There is no reason for you to use the excuse of age: you can sail. He ought to give thanks to us both: my brother brought me back to this man, I brought this man his brother. If you disowned him as a sluggard, he has sailed; if as undutiful, he has ransomed his own. What a son has received from the law cannot be snatched from him; for how can a father snatch away what he cannot but give?

The other side. Through the one I am compelled to disown the one I do not wish to. In this one thing the two please each other: that each displeases his father. Let us use the medicine to which we are driven, as is wont to be done with dangerous wounds — that the evil be cut out along with the body itself. Do you permit a young man to adopt, whom the law tests in the dividing of a patrimony? The law admitted you to the service of the patrimony, not to its ownership. Is there any age at which a man ceases to be a son? Not even to a thirty-year-old son is it permitted to adopt; for no one can take another into his own power who is himself in another's power. How can it be that you have the power of life and death over a brother, but not over a son? If he had deserved well of you, you would have begged your father on your brother's behalf. For that I did not ransom him was a matter of poverty: nothing was left in the common store; whatever the thirty-year-old had left, the disowned son had carried off. What was I to do, alone, an old man, helpless, whose patrimony one had divided and the other consumed?

The exile, father of the ravished woman. Let one condemned for unintentional homicide be exiled for five years. Let a ravished woman choose the death of her ravisher or marriage without a dowry. A man who had a daughter and a son, condemned for unintentional homicide, went into exile. His daughter was ravished; the ravisher betook himself to the girl's father; he obtained from him that he should bid his daughter choose marriage, and that he should give a letter to the son. On the brother's advice the girl chose death. The father returned; he disowns the son.

How shall I excuse myself to the commonwealth, from which I have taken two? Neither through my fault: in the one, fortune deceived me; in the other, my son. The daughter obeyed even her brother; the son obeyed not even his father. "By human errors," he says — I recognized my own prayers. "You can show all men," he says, "how unable you are to kill a man." You know I owe a citizen to the commonwealth: yet this difference there will be, that the unintentional we killed, the intentional we saved. I saw someone in exile beneath my own fortune.

The other side. He burst in insolently as into an exile's house. He reached the father, he did not spare his modesty. But I was complaining that he did the absent man an injury. I cannot be disowned for what was done by law. You could not, father, judge of an injury you did not know. Many things are wrung from us that we are unwilling to write. And you were in a fortune in which you could receive an injury, and he was the sort who could do an injury even in his own country. Because he knew his cause was bad, he pleaded it before one who did not know it. He returned proud, he bade us choose marriage, he compelled us; he seemed to have compelled in the same way there too. Yet by the letters he gained something: no one ever perished more slowly. He gathered a huge number of desperate men, stormed the house, harried the girl. This the ravisher had not told you.

Outside. Latro used to say that one who put forward another defendant in his own place was always hateful. Here the deed must not be diverted upon the sister's will. "One who defends," he said, "a charge is heard as a defendant; one who transfers it, as an accuser. But he is in a bad position who has the defendant's fortune and the accuser's odium." Asinius Pollio used to say that the colour should be shown in the narration, but carried through in the arguments. They acted unwisely who in the narration used up all the instruments of the colour; for they put more than the narration required, and less than the proof.

The brothers who were prizefighters. Let there be an action for ill-treatment. A certain man trained two sons as prizefighters; he brought them to Olympia. When they had been matched to fight together, the father came up to them as they fought and said he would disown the one who lost. The young men died together, and divine honours were decreed to them. The father is made defendant by his wife for ill-treatment.

You fought as a third without drawing lots, and conquered both. The father stood there, bloodstained; they had already perished, and still he threatened. They die not one by the other, but both by their father. The wretched mother cannot hate the man who killed her son. Young men unconquered, had they not had a father. Dutiful young men, you could not even refuse your father a parricide. They are unwilling to conquer, because of the parricide; unwilling to be conquered, because of the disowning. "I disown the one who is conquered." Madman, you will disown the better. I call upon Jupiter, whose Olympia have been cleared of parricide.

The other side. I did not mean to do it, and even if I meant to, I said it for the sake of glory. I ought not to be the only one in odium, when the loss is shared. All said the brothers would play at it together. I threatened not to lay fear upon my sons, but to satisfy the people.

The mother of the bastard chosen as a portion. Let the elder brother divide the patrimony, the younger choose. Let it be lawful to rear a son by a slave-woman. A certain man, who had a legitimate son, reared another by a slave-woman, and died. The elder brother divided thus, that he set the whole patrimony on one side, and on the other the mother of the bastard. The younger chose the mother and accuses his brother of fraud.

I alone of all men have been disinherited by the dividing. "He should have chosen the other portion," he says. You alone could be such a son as you are a brother. The law bade you divide, me choose: openly it fears lest the younger be defrauded. He divided thus, that, if I did not wish to be a beggar, I should leave my brother in want and my mother in slavery. It is not dividing, to set the patrimony on one side and a burden on the other. He was such a son that his father reared a co-heir for him by a slave-woman. Choose, so as to lack either the patrimony or the crime. Those are wont to be called defrauders who have carried something off: this man left nothing. "You yourself," he says, "wished to be poor." Why then do I complain, if I delight in want? "What was done by law," he says, "cannot be charged." Nay, nothing can be charged except what was done by law; for if anything was otherwise done, it is of itself void. Fraud always wraps a crime under the appearance of law: what is apparent in it is lawful, what lies hidden is insidious. Fraud always reaches injury through right. The law bids the elder divide, the younger choose: you did not divide, nor did this man choose; he was so bound by you that he must needs prefer what did not profit him. My devotion toward my mother was known; he did not fear that I could choose the other portion.

The other side. I did nothing but divide. The fraud is not in the division, but in the choosing. You have a mother whom some have ransomed with their whole goods; you have a glory that some have sought through fire, through arms. She carried off much of the patrimony, having, by a slave-woman's effrontery, the right of a mistress. Did you fear I would rage against her? It did not profit me, since in her I was about to have the whole patrimony. As it is, you have just as much; for you have the portion you wished. That you should have just as much, not even your father had wished; therefore he left your mother a slave.

The thrice-disowned man holding poison. A man thrice disowned and thrice acquitted was caught in a secret part of the house by his father holding a drug. Asked what it was, he said it was poison, that he wished to die; and he poured it out. He is accused of parricide.

Tell me what I have done: surely not even my secrets escape you. When my father came upon me, I had fallen into these thoughts: was anyone ever so unhappy? Does anyone hate me more than I hate myself? I began to pity myself. Three times I pleaded my cause; to these punishments of mine poison was added; I will live, if not even this is enough for you. Mithridates had poison, Demosthenes had poison.

The other side. Though he says he wishes to die, he asks for life. I hold a parricide prepared even for his own death. How small is what you deny, when so great is what you confess? You sought poison, you bought poison, you brought poison into that house in which you had a father who was your enemy. Tell who sold it; it will be said to him: did you sell poison to anyone? to a disowned man? Did you not know to whom he meant to give it? Do you ask for whom he prepared the poison? He did not drink it. What he denies is parricide; what he confesses is poisoning. "I prepared it," he says, "for myself" — that no one may doubt whether he can kill another . . . I say your father was so hateful to you that you wished to kill him; you yourself confess he was so hateful that you wished to die.

Outside. A double conjecture from a single person: whether he prepared it for himself, or for his father. The deified Julius brought Laberius forward at his games as a mime, and then restored him to the equestrian order. When he bade him go and take his seat, all the knights so crowded together that they would not receive him as he came. Caesar had then enrolled many in the senate, both to refill the order, drained by the civil war, and to return thanks to those who had deserved well of his party. Cicero, jesting at both things, said to Laberius as he passed: "I would have received you, if I were not sitting in a narrow space." Laberius sent back to Cicero: "And yet you are wont to sit on two stools." This because Cicero had a bad name as neither a sure friend to Pompey nor to Caesar, but a flatterer of both.

The man defamed concerning his daughter-in-law. The father of two young men gave one of them a wife; and while he was abroad, the father-in-law began to be defamed concerning the daughter-in-law. The husband, on returning, took off his wife's slave-girl and tortured her. She perished under torture. The husband, uncertain what he had been inquiring into, hanged himself. The father orders the other son to marry the same woman; when he refuses, he disowns him.

"Marry," he says, "your brother's wife." If this can be done, the brother found an adulterer. This is for me the cause of disowning, which for my brother was the cause of death. "Marry," he says, "your brother's wife." I believed, if there is any faith to be had, that I was being tested. Woman, if you can marry a man in mourning, you make all things be believed of you. I am compelled to marry the woman who is for me the cause of disowning, for the people of rumour, for my brother of death. I have already chosen a wife who, if travel abroad befall, would wish to travel with me; who, if anything befall her husband, would not wish to marry another. Those who hear that I am being disowned think my brother suspected something of me.

The other side. You have charged me with the utmost abomination, and one that a man who merely suspected it was unwilling to live with. At your urging my brother tortured the slave-girl, and because he found nothing, he expiated his false suspicions by death.

The man reclaiming one of two exposed children. Let things done by force and fear be invalid. Let agreements made according to the laws be valid. Let one who recognizes an exposed child take it back on repaying the cost of its rearing. A certain man took up two exposed children and reared them. To the natural father, who was seeking them, he promised to tell where they were, if he gave him one of the two. An agreement was made between them. He gives him back the two, and reclaims one.

When we divide our children with strangers, whom do we not divide with their mothers? I begot both, I longed for both, I bargained for both. Together they were born, together exposed, together reared; given back, they are torn apart. Fortune once tore them from their parents, never from each other. I exposed the two, because I could not choose between them. At an auction the hostile spear does not divide brothers, though it be hostile: it is something more to be twins than brothers; each loses his own grace unless he is with the other. Let him pardon me for keeping mine, since he himself covets another's. Shall recognition divide those whom even exposure joined? I bargain for everything for my son except my son. I bargained weeping, trembling, as when I exposed them. There was upon me then force and necessity; for I could not find my sons unless I promised one of them.

The other side. You can dismiss the father from this trial in both characters. This man is accustomed to be without children; but I, even when I have received one, must needs be tortured: I have grown used to two. Do you call force what made you a father? I took them up, I reared them, I gave them back; he is to choose. By this force I have lost two sons. The law embraces arms and chains and the utmost peril.

Outside. Against Clodius Sabinus, declaiming on one day in both Greek and Latin, many witty things were said. Haterius said, to certain men complaining that he took small fees, since he taught two subjects, that those who teach interpretations never take large fees. Maecenas said: "the son of Tydeus — you could not tell to which side he belonged." Cassius Severus, returning from hearing him and asked how he had spoken, answered: "badly, and in a bad way."

The madman because he forced his daughter to die. Let there be an action for madness. In the civil war a certain woman followed her husband, though she had her father and brother on the opposite side. When her own party was conquered and her husband killed, she came to her father, by whom she was not received, and said to her father: "How do you wish me to make satisfaction to you?" He answered: "Die." She hanged herself before his door. The father is accused by his son of madness. He speaks against it.

Not even the victor wished satisfaction to be made to him in this way. There was no head on the proscription-list of a woman. You have stained your household gods with your daughter's blood — though why do I speak of the household gods, as though she had perished in the house? Caesar wept over Pompey's head when it was brought to him; and he wept for this man over his daughter. "How do you wish me to make satisfaction to you?" By this very thing the girl ought to have made satisfaction, so dutiful both to her husband and to her father, that she followed the one even to death, and made satisfaction to the other even by death. I offend dangerously a father who knows not how to forgive. "Die." What else had she deserved, if she had refused to make satisfaction? You defended Ligarius, Cicero. How light a charge you judged that, of which you confessed! Before his very threshold she was extinguished, that it might not be doubted whether she had perished for her husband or her father. "She deserved it," he says. Do you accuse her even now? And surely satisfaction has now been made to you. The son-in-law followed the opposite side, the wife her own. The best defence in a civil war is forgetfulness. "Die," he says. Even those who must punish the condemned do not say, "kill," nor "die," but "act according to the law"; they soften the cruelty of the command with a milder word.

The other side. You owe it to your father to approve your character, not to rule his. You must gather many signs of madness; you cannot condemn a father for words. Manlius punished his son, and a victor at that; Brutus punished his children, who were not enemies made, but to be made. See whether, under these examples, a father may not be permitted only to speak more sternly. She asked stubbornly, and in what way she died: I recognized nothing of a daughter, nothing of a conquered woman. She did not send her brother to her father. Or is she even now angry at her brother? Why does she ask me alone, when she ought to make satisfaction to two? "The victor," he says, "was quickly won over." It is easier to forgive war than parricide. Even by her death she sought to stir up ill-will against her father. The woman is said to have perished for her father, who had one man for whom she could die.

The brave man without hands. Whoever catches an adulterer with the adulteress, provided he kills both bodies, shall be free of guilt. Let it be lawful to punish adultery in a mother and a son. A brave man lost his hands in war. He caught an adulterer with his wife, by whom he had a grown son; he ordered his son to kill the man. The son did not kill him; the adulterer escaped. He disowns his son. The son speaks against it.

I alone of all husbands neither let the adulterers go nor killed them. Who would not suppose either that I had no son, or that my son had no hands? This fellow was conceived — by whom, we shall learn when I have caught adulterers in the act. Then for the first time I felt that I had lost my hands. In war I lost my own hands; at home I lost my son's as well. As vainly did I run to my son as to a sword. He did not go to war, and refused his hands to his country before he refused them to his father. He fought for you to the point that he could not fight for himself. Young man, follow the men you let go. "I could not," he says, "kill my mother." That you may be the better excused, add your father too.

The other side. I thought it a second parricide to kill a mother before her father's eyes. Crimes are not always within our control, and merciful Nature weakens even fierce spirits. At the spectacle of so unlooked-for an outrage I was stunned in my whole body. Father, you lacked hands; I lacked everything. Before I came back to my senses, they were gone. The crime you were commanding was greater than the one you had caught in the act. If you exact of me anything beyond my strength, I will say: forgive me, I cannot. A father forgives a son who refuses a voyage, if he cannot bear the sea; he forgives one who does not follow the camp, if he cannot, even though the father himself be a soldier. Recite the law itself: "Let it be lawful for the husband, and lawful also for the son." Why does it name so many, unless it thinks there are some who cannot? The adulterers escaped between a crippled father and a stunned son.

The grandson got of a prostitute. A certain man disowned his son. The disowned son betook himself to a prostitute and got a son by her. Falling ill, he sent for his father; when his father had come, he commended the boy to him and died. The father, after his son's death, took the grandson into adoption. He is accused by his other son of madness.

A new kind of madness is charged against me: I should have been sane, had I not acknowledged my own. I kept waiting for someone to plead for the disowned man: none of his kinsmen dared, since his brother held back. His failing breath was sustained until my coming. I entered; his eyes, already sinking, he raised at my name, and held back his fleeing spirit. Into my lap he laid both his son and his last breath. It was told me that my son was at the point of death — and not by his brother.

The other side. This boy's father is uncertain: it would go well with him, if his mother too were uncertain. Among his other misfortunes he fell in with a prostitute — and a fertile one. I do not know whether the woman did the more wrong against the father in taking from him an heir or in giving him one. He adopted the son of the very woman for whose sake he had cast out his own.
Saved by his son. Let one who has been saved have no right of action against his saviour. A father who has been saved by his son disowns him. The son enters a plea in bar.

I might have been allowed to perish, if I am not allowed to speak. Do you think me saved? I was taken captive. Give me back to the enemy; captives are allowed to speak. Since he boasts so greatly of the gift of life, hear who gave it first. If anyone gives me back to the enemy, I will call him my saviour. Or do you think disowning an action at law? Even if it is an action, the law that speaks of one saved pertains only to outside persons, to son and father no more than to slave and master, freedman and patron. To depart from a father's power and come to the assessment of the favour: he who gives life, if he first received it, does not bind, but repays. I went into the battle line as an example to my son; not the enemy but age conquered me; he saved the one who had often saved him. A prostitute calls me an old man come back to life, I am matter for the jests of parasites; by all of them, as if they were my saviours, I am bidden to keep silent. Son, if I am not allowed to live, why was I not allowed to perish? "I shielded you," he says. So you, a young man, did not stand before your father in the line? Hear my son's glory: he did not commit parricide; when he could have saved me, he saved me.
The other side. This man begot me; he gave me my breath, he gave me these hands by which he was to be saved.

The man who conquered with the arms of a tomb. Let there be an action for a violated tomb. When there was war in a certain city, a brave man, having lost his own arms in the battle line, took the arms of a brave man from his tomb. He fought bravely and put them back. Having received a reward, he is accused of violating a tomb.

I had scarcely touched the arms; they followed me. If I take these, they are arms; if I leave them, they are spoils. You would have seen a tomb truly violated, had the enemy come there. Each of us lent what the other lacked: he gave arms to the man, I gave a man to the arms. The commonwealth gained much, the brave man lost nothing. It is necessity that lightens a ship by jettison, necessity that overwhelms fires by demolition: necessity is the law of the moment. Is nothing done lawfully on behalf of the laws? It went better with the very tomb, in which the victorious arms are now more renowned. For the commonwealth temples are often stripped, and we melt down their offerings for the use of soldiers' pay.

The other side. We have a defendant sluggish in battle, bold in flight, base no less in his defence than in his crime. He lost his own arms. This he could not excuse, unless he had snatched another's. He snatched another's. This he could not excuse, unless he had lost his own. Victorious arms, arms consecrated to the gods of the dead, arms that made you too a brave man. "I put back the arms," he says. He boasts that he did not lose these too. "I am not held by the law, because I put them back." You are held, by Hercules, as much as one who has wounded a man, even though he has healed the wound; as much as one who has stolen something, even though he has given it back when caught. This is not a crime to be remitted to him on account of his valour: we have already returned the favour to his valour; it has obtained its reward. We must be fair: we have honoured one brave man; let us avenge another.

The man condemned for parricide who binds his brother. Let one who has given false testimony be imprisoned in the house of the man against whom he gave it. Of two sons, the father set out with one; the young man returned alone. He was accused by his brother of parricide and condemned. Festal days intervening, his punishment was deferred by law; the father returned. The condemned man accused his brother of false testimony and won, and bound him. The father compels him to release the bound man; when he refuses, he disowns him.

"He gave false testimony," he says, "against his brother." If you wish to make his crime grave, show yourself open to entreaty.
