Cruel toward your brother, do you wonder if a parricide was believed of you? May I not, then, have two sons? Young man, you are now able even to commit parricide. One son was bound because I was not returning, the other because I returned. Will you never release your brother? If you are such a man, the witness lied in nothing: you are a parricide. He spoke not with a mind impious toward you, but pious toward your father: he held it suspect that you had left your father. I lie among my son's chains, shut in the same workhouse. Ingrate, you have bound your witness along with you.

The other side. Released at my peril, bound at my peril, he could scarcely have been released, had he given false testimony for his brother. He feigned a parricide concerning his father, and committed one concerning his brother. The executioner announced to me that my father had come. I am a parricide, as is charged, if I am even slightly angry with him. Do you wonder if I can bind the brother who could have killed me? The very deferral of my punishment was unwelcome: to wait seemed worse than to suffer; I pictured to myself the sack, the serpents, the deep.

The drink deadly in part. Let there be an action for poisoning. A wife followed her proscribed husband. At a certain time she asked him, as he held a cup in secret, what it was; he said poison, and that he wished to die. She asked him to give her a share, and said she did not wish to live without him. He drank part himself, gave part to his wife. She alone perished. By the will the husband was found heir. Restored, he is charged with poisoning.

He acted so as to be caught, was caught so as to be entreated, drank so as to live. What is this poison that harms only the heir? No one ever gave his wife poison so openly. He flees being killed, who says he longs to die. One man has been made richer by the proscription. To make him wish to live, his wife could not persuade him; a more alluring thing persuaded him, his wife's inheritance. He knew which part of the draught he was draining. The opposing party he pursued with the sword, his own with poison. The conquerors made an end of killing sooner than the conquered. What did you suppose would happen, when the wife had carried a will into exile, and the husband poison? Where is the wife? Are you not ashamed? Now even the proscribed return. As soon as she took the draught, she collapsed. Do not wonder if the poison is so effective: he is heir who gave it. Generally a light and harmless fluid hangs at the top, while that heavy and deadly part sinks by its own weight. It is plain that you had long had the poison prepared: you knew how to divide it. Even if one who gave it to a willing woman can be defended, can you, who made her willing? It was the kind of poison that, by its weight, sank to the bottom of the draught. This man drank as far as the poison, his wife drank the poison.

The other side. She loved her husband in peace, followed him in war, did not abandon him in his last counsel. O a woman worthy that I, innocent, should follow her! I waged civil war, I was proscribed, I went into exile; what can be added to these ills, except that I should drink poison and live? "It is poison," I said. Those who mean to give poison conceal it. Cato sold poison. Ask whether it was lawful for a proscribed man to buy what it was lawful for Cato to sell.

The blind mother holding back her son. Let children support their parents, or be imprisoned. A certain man, who had a wife and a son, set out and fell among pirates. He wrote to both about his ransom. The wife, by weeping, was made blind; she demands support of her son as he goes to the ransom; she wishes to bind him for not staying.

About to sail, he left his son to his wife, and she was not yet blind. There is no reason for you to assess the woman's feeling by the law with which she threatens; she does everything to keep her son from being bound. Whenever there is a common right between two, the power becomes wholly his who is present.

The other side. One woman binds two with chains. To the conquered the mother threatens fetters; the victor must go to the pirates. A son in his father's power, I can serve no one but my father. You demand support from the man whom his father sends abroad. The first claim is the father's, the second the mother's. He is abroad, you at home; he a captive, you free; he among pirates, you among citizens; he bound, you loosed. But you are blind. He is the more unhappy, in that he sees his own chains, and the slaughters and wounds and crosses of those who are not ransomed. But it is dangerous. How many have thought nothing dangerous for their fathers! "She seeks not vengeance," he says, "but mercy." Does anyone so exact filial love as to hinder it?

Outside. Calvus, who long had a most unequal contest with Cicero over the supremacy in eloquence, was so impassioned a pleader that, in the middle of his speech, Vatinius the defendant cried out: "I ask you, judges: if this man is eloquent, must I therefore be condemned?"
The man who killed himself. Let a homicide be cast out unburied. A certain man killed himself; it is demanded that he be cast out unburied. There is opposition.

He was driven to lay hands on himself by unrelenting ills. The sum of his misfortunes he removed in this, that he thought it was permitted a wretched man to die. Most unhappy young man, when I see you barred even from burial, I cease to wonder that you perished. You have such enemies that they pursue you even dead. Fortune conquers the wretched more easily than the wicked. Did you take up this blade, Cato — and how hateful it is, that you killed Cato? Curtius, you would have lost burial, had you not found it in death. What is more wretched in life than to wish to die? What in death than not to be able to be buried? Who would wonder that he wished to die, whom fortune pursues even in flight? Nature has given burial to all: the same wave that casts out the shipwrecked buries them; the bodies of those fixed to crosses flow down into their own burial; those who are burned alive are entombed by their punishment. Be angry at the slayer, but pity the slain. "He is a homicide," he says, "because he killed himself." Are you angry at this man? On whose behalf are you angry? Nothing else gave Mucius the name Scaevola, and left liberty to the city when he was captured before King Porsenna, but the cheapness in which he held himself; nothing else gave Codrus to the rest of generals as an example, but that, laying aside the insignia of a general, he ran to death, and was no greater general in anything than that he lied in saying he was not the general. I do not ask that it be glorious to die, but that it be safe. Those who kill men who wish to live are no more cruel than those who do not allow men who wish to die. Curtius, by casting himself into a chasm, mingled the destiny of burial with his fate; let Cato be celebrated: let only this be unpunished for this most wretched man, that he made some not ignoble decision about his own life. Even the wounds of the unhappy are scrutinized for a charge. Judge whether he was permitted to live, who was not even permitted to die.

The other side. It is an unworthy deed, if hands are found to bury the man whom their own killed. He took up the sword; I see his burning eyes — against whom, I do not know; this only I know, he is plotting a crime. Conscious of some crime I know not, he took refuge in death — a man among whose crimes is even this, that he cannot be condemned. Against such men it has been devised that those who do not fear death should fear something after death. He would have dared anything who could kill himself.

The man beaten by his son in the citadel. Let one who has beaten his father have his hands cut off. A tyrant summoned a father into the citadel with his two sons; he ordered the young men to beat their father. One of them threw himself headlong, the other beat him. Afterwards he was received into the tyrant's friendship. The tyrant being killed, he received the reward. His hands are demanded; the father defends him.

I should be happier if I were defending more defendants. Will you cut off the hands of a tyrannicide? What is this? The tyrant lies whole. It was as necessary to beat the father as to plunder temples, to ravish maidens. O how much we owe to these hands, through which now nothing is necessary! They were such that of them one could despise the tyrant, the other kill him. You threw yourself headlong, my son: this is not to spare your father but yourself. Endure, my son; against the tyrant you must go through your father. Which of my sons do you approve? One killed himself, the other the tyrant. He brought up his hands lightly and held back: the son feigned the blows, the father the groans. Necessity, the great defence of human misfortune: this excuses the Saguntines, though they did not beat their fathers, but killed them. Had it not been so . . . neither would this man have beaten me. The one had left me to my brother, this one to the tyrant. "In the law," he says, "nothing is excepted." But many things, though not excepted, are understood, and the letter of the law is narrow, the interpretation broad. What difference is there between excepting in the law that it be no offence in him who beat his father through madness, when he needs not punishment but a remedy, and that an infant be not punished if he beat his father? He who did this with the tyrant compelling was more wretched than the very man being beaten. She is not unchaste who was summoned by the tyrant; he is not a sacrilegious priest who carried the gifts of the immortal gods with his own hands to the tyrant. He did it at his father's bidding, and this man did not beat, but obeyed. The avenging of a beaten father belongs to none but the father. If I had been beaten by any stranger and were unwilling to bring an action for injury, no one would bring it in my name. As it is, there is no difference; the punishment of the man who beat me is greater, the right of the man who was beaten is the same.

The other side. He beat his father so long as it pleased him to be the tyrant's henchman. "I did it for the commonwealth." You charge the same thing to the commonwealth and to the tyrant. You had something to boast of to the tyrant: your brother chose to die; he perished that he might not commit a parricide, or see one. "Beaten, I remit the punishment." I should wonder, were there not, for so good a father, a son who wished to die. "My father wished it," he says. But my brother did not. "My father wished it," he says. So did you seem worthy of a parricide not only to the tyrant but even to your father? You beat your father, though you knew both the law and your brother.

Outside. From the proconsul Oppius, with whom Sabinus had gone to Crete, the Greeks in the theatre had begun to demand that Sabinus should hold the highest magistracy. Now it is the custom of the Cretans that the magistrate let his beard and hair grow. Sabinus rose, and silence being made by his hand, said: "This magistracy I have held twice at Rome." For twice, as a defendant, he had pleaded his cause. The Greeks did not understand, but, praying well to Caesar, asked that Sabinus might hold that honour a third time too. The same man, when as a defendant he begged to be transferred to the stone-quarries (lautumiae), said: "There is no reason for the very name of the lautumiae to deceive any of you; for that is a thing very far from being elegant (lautum)." He jested amid his own miseries and perils; and who does not know that he ought not to have jested in them — who believes that he could?

The maimed beggars. Let there be an action for harming the commonwealth. A certain man reared exposed children and, after maiming them, forced them to beg, so that they might bring him back their earnings. He is accused of harming the commonwealth.

It has come about that fathers neither acknowledge nor take back their children. His cruelty has been a source of revenue, all the more because all of us except him are merciful. It has been brought about that nothing is more wretched for the exposed than to be taken up, for parents than to acknowledge. The shoulder-blades of one, crushed, he beats out into a misshapen hump. Bring forth your household. I wish to know that workshop of human calamities. To each his calamity is assigned as if it were a trade. Look at one with his eyes gouged out, another with his feet broken. Why do you shudder? Thus does this man show mercy. A new monster: the whole man is fed, the maimed feed him. "They would have perished," he says. So do they not survive more unhappily? "They would have perished," he says. Ask the fathers which they would have preferred. How many brave men out of these, how many tyrannicides, how many future priests? Nor do I speak incredible things: out of this fortune the origin of the Roman race appeared. He enters his cruelty as more received than his mercy as expended. The exposed have been reared even by wild beasts, that would have been gentle enough, had they but passed by. Though their prayers are heard everywhere, in their own cause alone they fail. The tongue of one has been cut out, and it is a kind of asking to be unable to ask. Pity all of them, judges, each of whom singly you are wont to pity. Do you think we shall deny vengeance to these men, to whom we did not even deny what they were going to give you? A most unworthy thing: though he is so cruel, he lives by the public mercy. Rise up, wretched ones, and today for the first time ask for yourselves. "Your daily takings," he says, "do not come out right"; it is plain that you do not yet seem wretched enough. Dire omens will meet weddings, funereal auspices the public festivals, and on the days dedicated to mirth these half-living flocks wander about. They feed this man who cannot feed themselves. There is no one who does not know how to beg; he even teaches it. You have not so many limbs as you owe. So then, while you were thinking of the public mercy, could you be so cruel? Wretched those who beg thus, more wretched those who are begged thus! All bring an alms to all, while each man fears to refuse his own son. You have made it a greater evil to be reared than to be exposed. We feared wild beasts and serpents, and the cold hostile to tender limbs, and want too; among the dangers of the exposed we did not count the rearer.

The other side. "You maimed them," he says. Their fathers harmed them more. What of the trainer who forces young men to the sword, and yet is not accused of harming the commonwealth? What of the pimp who forces unwilling women to be defiled, and does not harm the commonwealth? I do not ask that the defendant be praised, but acquitted: let this harm him when he seeks offices; for a man can both not be an honourable man and be an innocent defendant. Though much was taken from them, their life was given back. An action for harming the commonwealth cannot be brought in the name of those who are outside the commonwealth. A needy man, who could feed neither myself, let alone others, I took up these abandoned ones, to whom no injury was done if something was taken from them, but who profited by the benefit if their life was saved. Let them stir up ill-will, let them say that they live so wretchedly through me, provided they confess that they live through me. By the mercy of one they live, by that of all they are fed. It is strange that men have leisure for this thought, to care what a beggar does among beggars. The leading men of this city employ their riches against nature: they have flocks of eunuchs; they cut their grown favourites, that they may be fit for a longer endurance of unchastity, and because they themselves are ashamed to be men, they take care that as few as possible be men. To these delicate and handsome cripples no one comes to aid. You care who carries off infants from the wilderness who would perish unless carried off; you do not care that these rich men cultivate their own solitudes with workhouses of the free-born, and, deceiving the simplicity of the most wretched young men, thrust down into the gladiator-school every one most handsome and most fit for the camp.

The ravisher of two women. Let a ravished woman choose either the death of her ravisher or marriage without a dowry. In one night a certain man ravished two women. One chooses death, the other marriage.

He is accused on the charge of outrage, and on the charge of outrage he is defended; he goes to law with one ravished woman, and calls upon the other to plead for him. Avenge it, fathers; let the severity of public discipline rise up the stronger; now they are ravished two at a time. The people gather as if struck by some public terror, scarcely able to believe there was one ravisher of two. He ravished one to do her injury, the other to win his defence. You would already have perished, ravisher, had you not deserved to perish twice over. If he had ravished you first and you had chosen marriage, and then he had violated this woman before you were wed, would you deny that he must die at the bidding of the woman he ravished? You can do nothing more for the ravisher than to keep him from perishing by your own law; against another's law you have no right. You grant the ravisher that you yourself do not kill him; you cannot grant that no one kill him.

The other side. Between verdicts that are equal, let the gentler win. Cite Verginia, name Lucretia: still the Sabine women are more in number. It will be an affront to me, that you are judged worthy to have a man killed for your honour, while I am judged unworthy to have one saved for mine.

The wife tortured by the tyrant on her husband's behalf. A wife, tortured by a tyrant as to whether she knew anything of her husband's plot against him, persisted in denying it. Afterwards her husband killed the tyrant. Within five years he divorced her, since she bore no child, on the ground of barrenness. She brings an action against him for ingratitude.

The marriage which the tyrant did not part, the tyrannicide has parted. Married women were dragged off, virgins were carried away; none then seemed more fortunate than those who had no children. The tyrant suspected this man of plotting his death, whether something slipped from him or his face did not well conceal great designs; yet he cannot complain of his wife's tongue, since he knows how she keeps silent. Set upon the rack, she looked back more often to her absent husband than to the tyrant before her eyes. The whole apparatus of tyrannic cruelty is unrolled against the unhappy woman, and those instruments that break the very spirits of men by the mere sight of them are set out to wring from her the knowledge in a woman's breast; her body is torn apart with stripes. I do not know, commonwealth, whether that woman will give you children; she gave you a tyrannicide. Do you wonder if five years passed between a tortured wife and a busy husband? Her body slit with whips, scorched with fire, racked with torments — you will pardon the woman, I think, if I say: she is weary. Why do you boast of tyrannicide? It is easier to kill a tyrant than to endure one. Whips, hot plates, the rack, whatever ancient savagery had devised, whatever the new age had added — what more shall I say? The tyrant tortured her even when he was inquiring about tyrannicide. Does she burden your purse, costly in her expenses, and, as the way of the age is — luxury flowing ever to the worse — does a woman's vanity rage in mutual rivalry to the point of public harm by private extravagance? Does she ask for gems and little stones sought from a foreign shore? Wait, she can yet bear a child; fertility does not answer to a fixed day. Nature is her own mistress. Which do you think the more to be wondered at — your tyrannicide or her silence?

The other side. "I was tortured." You would justly reproach me with it, had I not avenged you. Even if you knew of your husband's tyrannicide and did not betray it, it is no service not to commit a crime. And besides, you did not know; for I did not tell you, nor did I entrust so great a design — heavy even for the spirits of men — to a woman's chatter, which can keep silent only about what it does not know. At the time my wife was tortured I was thinking nothing yet of tyrannicide; afterwards I thought of it, and this very thing, the avenging of my wife, was my reason for thinking of it. If she kept silent about what she had heard, it is no service but mere good faith.

Outside. Lucius Vinicius, than whom no Roman citizen had a readier talent in pleading cases. Whatever long reflection was to furnish him, the first effort of his mind gave; he pleaded cases extempore, yet he did not desire this commendation — that he should seem to plead extempore. Of him the deified Augustus elegantly said: "Lucius Vinicius keeps his talent in ready cash."

The father who keeps back the ravished woman. Let a ravished woman choose either the death of her ravisher or marriage without a dowry. The ravisher demands that the ravished woman be brought forth. Her father is unwilling.

He is the ravisher, and I am hauled into court. It is not so easy for an honest man to kill as for a desperate one to die. "The law," he says, "is common to both." May the gods grant that you do not force me to try whether all of it is mine. "When, then," he says, "will she make her choice?" At this time she cannot; I am tending her wounds, I am restoring my household, I am mourning my stormed house, I am consoling her ravished virginity, I am guarding one who threatens her own life. When will she choose? When the ravished woman wishes, not when the ravisher. When will she choose? When you do not wish it. "When," he says, "will she choose?" I am preparing myself for the choice, I am steeling my mind; it is not easy to kill a man; meanwhile I press down my groans and drive inward the tears that burst forth. You know what will happen: my face has deceived you. Fool, do you think anyone delays his daughter's marriage? You run upon the axe and call the executioner of your own accord. When you ought to be begging, you offer insult. No one is compelled to avenge himself.

The other side. Nothing is more wretched than to be left in doubt between life and death. It will now be a kindness, even if she chooses death. I fell in love with this man's daughter. I should have approached the father about marriage; I did so; but you see how, even in respect of the law, he is slow. The ravisher has his life at another's discretion, his liberty at his own. This law is common to both. This ravisher has something to fear, and something too that he may hope for. "In the law," he says, "it is not written when." Nay, at once; whenever a time is not added, the present is understood. Shall so long a right over a citizen's life be permitted you? It is crueller than to die — always to fear death.

The stepson who is a physician. A certain man disowned his son. The disowned son studied medicine. When the father was ill and the physicians said he could not be healed, the son healed him. He was taken back. Afterwards the stepmother began to be ill; the physicians despaired. The father asks his son to treat the stepmother. When the son refuses, he disowns him. The son speaks against it.

By what arrangement did it come about that at my disowning my father fell ill, and at my return my stepmother? The diseases yielded to filial devotion. I leave off medicine, much toil, much wakefulness; add to this that those who are healed are ungrateful. As a physician I may be deceived, and as a stepson I cannot be excused. "The physicians say," he says, "it is the same disease" — those, namely, who said you could not be healed. But I leave the house, if you grant that she can be healed thus. I fear fortune. It will be laid to my charge if anything happens. See, you yourself do not believe that I am unable. All the physicians deny it, and now they have been more careful, because in your case they were deceived. I am not of so great skill as I seem: great teachers are needed; I, a disowned man, studied. Do you ask how I healed you? I helped you not as a physician but as a son; you were suffering from longing; whatever you received from my hands was pleasing to you. As soon as I entered, you were revived: I noticed what in you needed healing. She does not suffer from the same disease. Many things are unlike: sex, age, temperament. Nothing profits the sick more than to be treated by the one they wish. Grave diseases are cured by bold remedies, which I do not dare to use on a stepmother.
Outside. A young man ought to bear no grudge against his stepmother; otherwise he both hates and rejoices. A young man is to be borne with if he excuses himself; not if he takes revenge.

The other side. There is cause for mourning, for weeping; was it for this you saved me? An enemy once healed a wound he had made, chiefly because no other could heal it. They say she cannot be healed. No one undertakes it; for no one wishes to snatch the treatment from a son.
Outside. Pollio used to say: between fathers and sons the judge thinks only that lawful which is fitting.

The house burned along with the tree. Let one who has knowingly done damage pay fourfold; one who has done it unknowingly, the simple amount. A rich man asked his poor neighbour to sell him a tree which he said stood in his way. The poor man refused; the rich man set fire to the plane-tree, and with it the house burned too. For the tree he offers fourfold, for the house the simple amount.

Roused by the sound of the flames, I first tested the good faith of my neighbours. The tree, with its branches running out, had covered the whole house. "He cannot be entreated; let it be burned." This is the mark of one without self-control, to covet without end, to be angry without measure. "He cannot be stormed by prayers; let him be driven out by fire." There is no difference between you and a poor man, if we proceed by law. Let even a poor man be allowed to enjoy a prospect. You possess the territories of cities, and fill cities with your houses; within your buildings you enclose waters and groves. Nothing more elegant meets your eyes than my ruin. I have lost a house, I who could not do without even a little tree. Rich man, shall we burn for your delights? In a fire, pleasure is sought for the eyes, and a prospect is opened up by flames. "It blocked the prospect." What? As we walk, do not troops of slaves block us? Do not walls raised to an immense height shut out the light? Do not promenades stretched over endless spaces, and houses built upon the ground of whole cities, all but shut us off from the public street? Beneath this little tree I imagined to myself the forests of the rich. How much have I lost, whom even my angry enemy admits to have lost more than he wished? I make no unfair demand: let the fire end with the loss of the man whose plan it began with. Doubtless, that houses turned to face the whole sky may have wintry heats and summer chills, and that the year, against its own turns, may be driven within these men's homes, they nourish on their topmost roofs lying groves and the straits of navigable fishponds. Lands once ploughed for whole peoples are now the workhouses of single men, and overseers rule more widely than kings. Seas are pushed back by jutting moles. Did you not know how great is the power of fire, how irrevocable, how it consumes whole cities, from how slight beginnings fires arise? Even if you did not wish to do part of the damage, yet if you wished to do part, you must be held for the whole, as if you had done it knowingly; for he who is defended on the ground of ignorance must have been wholly unwilling. If you were to admit that you knowingly set fire to the door, to a single beam, I think the whole house would be understood from the part; for no one sets fire to everything, but to some one thing, from which the fire rises to scatter itself over all. And yet a tree that is in a house is part of the house.

The other side. The tree made my house unhealthy: it had blocked the whole sky through which a wholesome breath could come. I asked the poor man and said: "The tree, cut down, does you no harm; uncut, it does me very much. What are those branches to you that are outside the house?" The branches were pressing on certain parts of my house; they had already even shifted some of the walls. You know how great is the force of trees; they shatter walls.

Iphicrates as defendant. Let one who has done violence in a trial be punished with death. Iphicrates, sent against the king of the Thracians, twice conquered in the line, struck a treaty with him and married his daughter. When he had returned to Athens and was pleading his cause, certain men in Thracian dress were seen, armed, around the court, and the defendant himself drew his sword. When the judges were summoned to give judgement, they openly cast votes of acquittal. He is accused of having done violence in the trial.

Not one of your judges but feared as though you were going to judge them. He came as advocate with his whole kingdom; he did not array his war with greater forces than his trial. Iphicrates, sheathe your sword; it is a trial. What have you to do with a sword? Surely those twice conquered must lay down their arms. What is this exchange against the nature of things — a wedding in war, a war in a trial?

The other side. I did no violence; for all the lawful forms were carried out: the accuser spoke in his place, the defendant answered in his; the trial was completed in all its parts. While the judges were casting their votes, I drew my sword, to kill myself if I were condemned. The judges cast their votes of acquittal openly, to return thanks to their general. The reason for the marriage was the advantage of the commonwealth. The soldier had rather often been beaten in an unlucky battle. The barbarians around the court were armed not for any service, but after their own custom. "What," he says, "can you complain of? That I brought you a hostage?"

The five-year-old witness against the agent. A certain man, his wife being dead, by whom he had a son, married another; he reared a son by her. He had a handsome agent. When the stepmother and stepson often quarrelled, he ordered the boy to move out; he rented a dwelling across the wall. There was a rumour of adultery between the mother and the agent. At a certain time the father was found killed in his bedchamber, the wife wounded, the common wall pierced through. It pleased the kinsmen to ask the five-year-old son, who had slept with them, whom he recognized as the slayer; he pointed at the agent with his finger. The son accuses the agent of homicide; the agent accuses him of parricide.

When I heard the cry, if there is any faith to be had, I believed adulterers had been caught. Give me the boy. Is anyone not content with one witness? Give me the people. He charges the stepson with parricide, the son with a lie. Tell, boy, who killed your father; tell boldly; you name the same man as the people. Night suits crime, the time for adultery. O the great perversity of the age into its opposite! There was found a man who could kill his father, but could not kill his stepmother. Show me this — not a wound, but a proof; show me the wound: how the slayer feared to kill her! Did that right hand wound you so lightly, which neither the wall nor the father withstood? Nothing is more sure than a boy as witness; for he has reached the years at which he understands, and not those at which he invents.
Outside. Vinicius, a man of the most exact talent, could neither say silly things nor bear them.

The brave man unwilling to return to his brave father. A certain man disowned his son; the son kept silent. He did a brave deed; he sought his return to his father as a reward; the father spoke against it. Afterwards the father did a brave deed; he seeks his son's return to him; the son speaks against it.

I am the braver: after your battle we fought, after mine we conquered. Return; I have made the house worthy of you. These eyes are mine, these hands are mine, this stubbornness is mine. If I deserve the reward, give it to me; if I do not deserve it, give him his own. "I," he says, "did not take a reward under the same law." This is why you were disowned, that you think there is no difference between you and your father. After deeds so alike, if you were only a fellow-soldier, you ought to have adopted me as your father. I warn you, young man: he who had refused this reward now seeks it. "I fear you will disown me again." Do you think I will let it come about that I beg twice? I fought in a graver war, in which even old men had to serve, in which even those who had been brave in the former war could not be brave. He exercised his own years; I conquered mine. You broke the war; I ended it. How great an exhortation to the young I was, a brave old man! Give back to each of us his reward. I served as an old man, I served drained of blood, I served when I had already given a substitute. Each of us, when he is asked, scorns it; when he is forsaken, asks for it. Why do you force us to suspect, in that you will not come into your father's house except by your own reward? It was disgraceful that a brave man should not be received except by a father compelled to it.

The other side. Why do you wish to make me a captive out of a free man? Why do you subject a brave man to disgrace? Why do you bring it about that he can be disowned? "You are my son," he says. What need of a reward, if I am yours?

The stepson carried off from the stepmother by his grandfather. Let there be an action for force. A certain man lost two sons under a stepmother, with doubtful signs of indigestion and of poison. The maternal grandfather, who had not been admitted to visit the sick, carried off the third son. To the father, who was seeking him, he said through a herald that he was with him. He is accused of force.

I had a daughter, fertile, though only one son survives. Let him be reared with me. What do you fear? That you will not be admitted when you come? You do not seek the sons you lost; you seek the one you have not lost. The father reclaims one from me, I two from the father. I have more reason to fear as a grandfather than as a defendant. I came to my sick grandsons; I was not admitted: this was the true force. There is no force which has not arms, a fight, wounds. Describe this man's retinue of tumult: there is one boy and one old man. "You carried off," you say, "my son." Nay, I took up my grandson; nay, I could not shut him out as he came. If I had snatched with an armed band the wife and children of a man besieged by robbers, could my benefit be made a charge? Even physicians bind us, and heal our bodies by force. He cannot deal with me as with a stranger. Nature has her own rights, and this is the difference between a grandfather and a father, that to a grandfather it is permitted to save his own, to a father even to kill. What is this devotion so late, so out of order? You begin to seek your own from the third. Whoever favoured the boy wished that he not be found.

The other side. He did it not to save his grandson, but to defame his wife with poisoning, and me as made over to a poisoner. Between me and my father-in-law, judges, there was no agreement even while my former wife lived; but when she was dead, having declared himself my enemy, while the boy was failing, with outcry and abuse, ill-boding whatever happened, he came, who had never come before to his grandsons when they were well. I did not admit him; for then too I saw he came to carry off the boy.

Outside. Montanus has this fault: he spoils his sayings by repeating them, while, not content to say one thing well once, he brings it about that he has not said it well. For this reason Scaurus used to call Montanus the Ovid among orators; for Ovid too does not know how to leave off what has gone well. When Polyxena had been led to the tomb of Achilles to be sacrificed, Hecuba said: "the very ash of the buried man makes war on this our race." He might have been content; he added: "even from the tomb we have felt the enemy." And not content with this, he added: "for the son of Aeacus I was fruitful." Scaurus used to say that it is no less great a virtue to know how to speak than to know how to leave off.

Parrhasius and Prometheus. Let there be an action for harming the commonwealth. Parrhasius the Athenian painter, when Philip was selling the captive Olynthians, bought one old man; he brought him to Athens, then tortured him; after the model of the tortured man he painted a Prometheus. The Olynthian died under torture. Parrhasius set up the picture in the temple of Minerva. He is accused of harming the commonwealth.

The old man, dragged from his children, stood over the ashes of his burned country: he is sad enough to serve as model for a Prometheus. No one ever sank a man to paint him as shipwrecked. The Olynthian's last entreaty was: give me back to Philip. "He was my slave," he says. You would think it was Philip speaking. We flee the temple of Minerva as though it were the camp of the Macedonians. "He is not sad enough," he says. Is any Olynthian not sad enough? Do you wish, Parrhasius, to see a sad man? Lead him to Olynthus as it lies in ruins. You know well how sad a man you bought. To the Olynthians we opened our city, our temples we shut. No Olynthian would have been tortured, had all the Macedonians bought them. "Let him be tortured" — this not even under Philip. "Let him die" — this not even under Jupiter. So hospitable was this man to the Olynthian. This is to make a Prometheus, not to paint one. "I bought him," he says. Nay, if you are an Athenian, you ransomed him. In this temple we took up vows for the Olynthians. That butcher of Greece nevertheless did no more to this man than sell him. An old man, consumed by the long wasting of his miseries, and as sad as if he had already been tortured. Whomever the auctioneer had seen weeping, he recognized as the buyer. I fear that someone, when he hears of the Olynthian's stripes, tortures, fires, may think I am complaining of Philip. If you believe this man, he imitated an angry Jupiter; if you believe us, he outdid an angry Philip. As much must be suffered with Parrhasius painting as with Jupiter angry. Most wretched old man, perhaps some one of your slaves serves more happily. If you set out to bring aid, I complain that you bought only one; if to torture, I complain that you bought any. On one side stands Parrhasius with his colours, on the other the torturer with his fires: Parrhasius is in doubt between them, whether to paint more eagerly or to rage. The old man is brought forward, looking back at his country; his unhappy face pleased Parrhasius. The Olynthian had something like Prometheus even before the tortures. Fire, tortures, the sword: is this the workshop of a painter or of Philip?

The other side. Never is public repute corrupted by the harm of one man. The opinion of the Athenians is too solid to be shaken by the tortures of a captive. "You harmed the commonwealth," he says, "in that you set up this picture in the temple." They harm the commonwealth who take something from it, not who add to it. Did the priests, then, sin by receiving the picture too? Yet why should they not receive it? The crimes of the gods are painted in temples. Much has always been permitted to the arts: physicians, to learn the unknown force of a disease, have cut open the entrails of men.

The pirate chief's daughter. A man captured by pirates wrote home about his ransom; he was not ransomed. The pirate chief's daughter made him swear to take her as his wife if he were set free. He swore. Leaving her father, she followed the young man. He married her. He came into a childless inheritance. His father orders him to dismiss the pirate chief's daughter and marry the childless heiress. When he refuses, the father disowns him.

A wife of good hope, a daughter-in-law of good hope, who can love even a captive, and hate even a father. "I lay," he says, "in prison and in darkness." Tell me, I beg, the kindnesses of your father-in-law. The girl was moved not by pity but by lust.

The other side. She did not abandon me in a place into which even my father feared to come. You would have seen my limbs crushed by chains, my eyes shrunken and drawn inward with wasting, my hands worn by the fetters and useless: who but a merciful woman could love such a man? In all his consulships Marius has nothing more glorious than that he was his own founder. If hereditary portraits had carried Pompey aloft, no one would have called him the Great. Rome bore Servius as her king. What do you make of those men called from the plough, who by their own poverty made the commonwealth blessed? We cannot be fortunate together: what is our custom, we shall be unfortunate together.
The dissolute father and son. A certain man, while his son lived in dissipation, began to live in dissipation himself. He is accused by his son of madness. The father speaks against it.

My accuser has within him conflicting feelings: he longs that the defendant be condemned and the charge acquitted. "But you are an old man," he says; this is what you mean: my dissipation began later and will end sooner. Some have said that the highest good is pleasure. I have no need of those who lay down precepts; I have an example. I have shown you the dissipation in yourself that you did not see in yourself. Drunk, you charge your father with drunkenness.

The other side. A young man who is dissolute sins; an old man who is dissolute is mad. No one imitates vices because he hates them. What general ever fled the battle himself, that his army might fight well? He does not check vices who provokes them. I too shall lay my own dissipation to my father's charge. I was not under a strict discipline, not under the rule of a well-ordered house, which might have formed a young man's character and led him away from the vices of his age. In a sense I was sent ahead to dissipation by my father. Grey hairs dripping with perfume, and an old reveller, are too dissolute for no one, but seem to no one quite sane.

The house burned along with the tyrant. Let there be an action for damage done. A certain man, while pursuing a tyrant who was fleeing from the citadel, drove him into a private house. He set fire to the house: the tyrant was burned up along with the house. He received a reward. The owner sues him for the damage.

Whom did you shut out and whom did you take in? Why did the tyrant make for no other house? Everyone shut his house against him as he came. I had no entrance into the house, who had one into the citadel. Do you not rejoice to have spent something on the public liberty? "This is the man in whose house the tyrant was killed." You are pointed out as a tyrannicide. "Give me back my house," he says. So while the tyrant lived you had not lost it? The tyrant's friend, the tyrant's henchman, certainly — what you cannot deny — his host. Long I waited to see whether the tyrant would be cast out. You can more easily accuse either yourself, who were so intimate with the tyrant that your house most of all pleased him, who took him in; or the tyrant, who did you the damage in fleeing into your house; or, that I may free you from blame, you can more easily accuse fortune, which brought the tyrant to you of all men.

The other side. The damage ought to be his whose the reward is. It is not unfair that the wrong of that thing be charged to you, the fruit of which you have reaped. The tyrant did not choose the house — for he had no leisure for that — but burst into the one he could, when I was not in it. This man, having found an occasion of doing harm, would not enter, but chose a tyrannicide that was doubtful, slow, dangerous to the city. He received a reward, no doubt the greater, as if he ought to make good the damage.

The indistinguishable son and stepson. A certain man, his wife being dead, who had perished in childbirth, married another; he sent the boy to the country. By her in time he got a son. He brought up both boys in the country; after a long time they returned, alike. When the mother asks which is hers, he does not tell her. He is accused by her of ill-treatment.

Why do you weep, boys? Be at ease; I do not remember. Already there are lawsuits, and I have not yet told. What kind of stepmother will you be, who so long to become one? One is yours, the other is your son's brother, and if you would permit it, neither is a stepson. While you wish to be mother of the one, you are stepmother of both. If you compel me, I will lie: not as a mother but as a stepmother you will be deceived. These two Nature herself willed not to be distinguished. I would tell, were you not so stubbornly asking. This one is yours. Why do you look at the other with a stepmother's eyes? That one is yours. To you alone has it fallen to have a stepson and not be a stepmother.

The other side. She sues for ill-treatment; for the son was banished to the country by the father and brought up so that he could be unknown even to his mother. To you both have returned as sons, to her both as stepsons; she is the more cruelly without a son, the nearer she has come to him. You fear her unfairness, when, unfair yourself, you love more the one to whom you wish to give another's mother than the one to whom you do not wish to give back his own.

Outside. As to the husband's colour, Romanius Hispo and Pompeius Silo used this: "I do not know, and therefore I do not tell." Some mixed the two and, using both, said: "I do not know, but even if I knew I would not tell" — which Latro and Cestius used. But Asinius Pollio approved neither colour. "If he says, 'I do not know,'" he said, "he convinces no one: the wife herself would not be asking him, unless he could know." For it can be said against the husband: "Ask the nurse, ask the tutor; it is not likely that no one is in the house who knows." But that mixed colour spoils both — the credibility of one who is ignorant, and the confidence of one who will not tell. For when he says, "even if I knew, I would not tell," he makes the judge think he does know; when he says, "I do not know," he makes it seem that he ought to tell, if he knows. He himself, however, used this colour, which he called the simplest: "I know, but I do not tell, because this is useful for the boys"; and to your son: "I shall love more the one who will seem to have no mother."

The man carried off in woman's dress. Let an unchaste man be barred from the public assembly. A handsome young man made a wager that he would go out into public in a woman's dress. He went out; he was carried off by ten young men. He accused them of violence and got them condemned. Barred from the assembly by the magistrate, he makes the magistrate defendant for injury.

He put on a woman's dress, arranged his hair in a woman's style, encircled his eyes with girlish allurement, coloured his cheeks. Do you not believe it? Even those who had not believed it lost their wager, and perhaps it came of the wager that he dared, an unchaste man, to address the assembly. Give him a girl's dress, give him night: he will be carried off. The dress, once put on, so became him that he seemed not to have put it on then for the first time. The deeds of his whole youth I pass over; I am content with one night: so well did he imitate a girl that he found a ravisher. Did I strike anyone? Did I compose a defamatory song, or — to call it by the special name of the injury done you — did I carry you off? Among our forefathers, a man who entered upon his service in the courts thought it wrong to bare his arm from the toga. How far from these manners were men who used even their virtue so modestly? It is agreed that this man was outraged, since those who carried him off were condemned.

The other side. It is agreed that he was always grave, always serious; but this was done by the jests of young men. For the rest, his modesty was so well known that no one would now believe it without a wager.

The adulteress and poisoner. Let there be an action for poisoning. A certain man who had a wife and by her a marriageable daughter told his wife to whom he meant to give her in marriage. She said: "She will die sooner than marry that man." The girl died before her wedding day, with doubtful signs of indigestion and of poison. The father tortured a slave-girl; she said she knew nothing of poison, but knew of an adultery between her mistress and the man to whom he meant to give the daughter. He accuses his wife of poisoning and adultery.

"She will die" — I have the poisoner; "sooner than marry" — I have the adulteress. "She will die" — it was done; "sooner than marry" — it was done. The adultery I detected later than it was done, the poisoning before it was done. Two crimes I have brought before you, and two informers: one tells what has been done, the other even what is to come. To her son-in-law an adulteress, to her daughter a rival. How unhappy is the house in which adultery is the proof! I said, "He is honourable"; I said, "He is handsome"; while I praised the son-in-law, I recommended the adulterer. O how slow I am in my own misfortunes! The poisoning, even when foretold, I did not believe; the adultery I detected only in the poisoning. The wedding was turned into a funeral, the marriage-bed changed into a bier, the happy torches set beneath the pyre. The body is brought forth, rotting and swollen with poisons. What more do you ask? The signs agree with the words, the tortures with the signs. The deeds agree with your voice. "She will die before she marries" — it was done. We saw the flowing body, and in her corpse we believed the mother's words. I lost my son-in-law by adultery, my wife by parricide, my daughter by poisoning.

The other side. He has charged two most grievous crimes, adultery and poisoning: the adultery on a slave-girl's testimony, the poisoning not even on a slave-girl's. When she was indignant at not being consulted, words slipped from her — words of one who mourns her daughter no less than he does. But why did you say, "She will die sooner than marry that man"? Words slipped out, too little considered in grief. And very often divination is fortuitous.

The madman who joined his daughter to a slave. A tyrant gave the slaves leave to ravish their mistresses. The leading men of the city fled, and among them one who had a son and a daughter. When all the slaves had violated their mistresses, this man's slave saved the maiden. The tyrant being killed, the leading men returned; they crucified the slaves; this man freed his slave and joined his daughter to him. He is accused by his son of madness.

We would have a solace, if the tyrant had made this marriage, not the father. Do you think him sane who chose to imitate a tyrant rather than a slave? He made himself like a tyrant, his daughter like the ravished, his freedman like the crucified. The master allowed his slave more than the tyrant did. Whoever makes this marriage is either mad or a tyrant. A noble son-in-law, who has nothing more glorious about him than that he is not among the crucified. Under her father she lost the virginity she had saved under the tyrant. Is he then worthy of marriage, because he is unworthy of the cross? The lot of the violated is better than the maiden's: to them it fell to change their marriages. A propitious father gave his daughter in marriage as an angry tyrant gave the daughters of others. When the father was sane, he fled that he might not see this marriage. Most wretched sister, under the tyrant you longed for your father; under your father you long for the tyrant. Is it not a reward for him, alone to look upon the crosses of all? He did not violate his mistress. Heap up his kindnesses: he neither killed his master nor gave poison. It is no kindness to abstain from crime. What others suffered under the tyranny, this woman suffered in freedom; the rest while their kinsmen were absent, she while hers were present; in others it is called defilement, in her marriage. He feared punishment; he knew the commonwealth would be freed, that those who had defiled would pay the penalty; and he saw the last hour drawing near for the tyranny. Gather, little slaves; gather, freedmen — a bought kinship.

The other side. If anyone had informed the tyrant, this man alone would have hung on the cross. I may give my daughter in marriage to whom I will. Marcus Cato married the daughter of his tenant. My daughter will not fear a husband's insolence, nor abusive words, nor a rival, nor divorce. Nature made no one free, no one a slave; fortune afterwards laid these names upon individuals. Lately we too were slaves. A slave was a king.

The poor shipwrecked man, the rich man's father-in-law. Let a violated woman seek either the death of her violator or marriage without a dowry. A rich man solicited a poor man three times about marriage with his daughter; three times the poor man refused. Setting out with his daughter, he was cast by shipwreck onto the rich man's estate; the rich man approached him about marriage with his daughter; the poor man kept silent and wept. The rich man held the wedding. They returned to the city. The poor man wishes to bring the girl forward to the magistrate. The rich man speaks against it.

Let the girl be brought forward to the magistrate. What do you fear? Surely she is your wife. You will not even be able to complain of death, if the girl chooses it. No ravisher ever perished later. As I recognized the shore, shipwrecked, I swam out to sea. What do you fear, if you won her father over? He came to me first; "I wish," he said, "to marry your daughter." I did not weep; for then it was permitted to refuse. I wept over my daughter's wedding as over my own shipwreck. Shipwrecked, I complain more of the shore. Between the shipwreck and the wedding not even one night intervened. Put off the wedding until the father-in-law leaves off weeping. He thinks I have already entrusted my daughter to him, when this man does not yet entrust himself to a wife. I come with tears flowing among my words: such was I at my daughter's wedding too. If she was ravished, why do you refuse her the choice? If she is a wife, why do you fear? I speak as soon as it is permitted. I had left my country far out of sight, yet I had not yet passed the rich man's estate; suddenly the sea bristled with waves, and the winds, at strife, blew to our destruction; night was sent down from the sky, and the day is given back only by lightnings; between sky and earth we hung in doubt. Yet so far, judges, we sail well; a greater shipwreck awaits on shore. There was, on the highest of the mountain ridges, the rich man's lofty watchtower: there he reckoned up the leavings of shipwrecks, there his unhappy revenue, and how much the angry sea gave back to him. I am asked about my daughter's wedding, while still the wave beat upon my ears; I did what I ought: captive and shipwrecked, I refused the defilement to my enemy with tears. A delicate rich man, who can love even amid shipwrecks. You hide the celebration of a marriage in the corner of a remote countryside; there you hold the wedding where no one comes but the shipwrecked. A tear is always the sign of an unwished-for thing; tears are the pledges of the unwilling, and the face is the index of a resisting mind. No one ever weeps over what he longed for. Tears are the bursting forth of a grief forced within the breast and of an intolerable silence. So he who weeps over his patrimony upon its ashes hates the fire; so he who weeps over a shipwreck detests the seas. Weeping is the modest cursing of human necessities. Now the part is yours, girl; I withdraw, and what I did before, I keep silent. If you are wedded, you have what to choose; if violated, what to command.

The other side. A shipwrecked man two things most sacred among men received: hospitality and kinship; the one I gave, the other I even asked for. The marriage being offered by the reconciling of fortune, I asked for it often, as a lover; I did not put it off, as one in haste. What of the ravisher is here, except that I married her without a dowry? The father-in-law errs who thinks the girl will be dearer to me if she can kill me. For what is left? My prayers, which I employed so often, or this man's tears, which I moved? My enemy can charge me with nothing but the marriage. Great is the love that comes from pity. We poured forth tears out of repentance for our former parting, and minds taken up with joys did not suffer either me to say more or him to answer more. No integrity, however well proved to itself, has so much confidence as to wish to plead its cause. If you question your daughter, you will be charging her with part of the law; if you do not question her, with the law. If he meant to give his son-in-law life, he would even have left him his innocence. Do you ask what he did while he wept? He did not refuse; and he was wont to refuse, if he were unwilling. He will choose death; for he cannot want those parts of the law that he has.

The daughter privy to the poisoning of her stepson. Let a poisoner be tortured until she names her accomplices. A certain man, his wife being dead, by whom he had a son, married another and by her got a daughter. The young man died; the husband accused the stepmother of poisoning. Condemned, while she was being tortured, she named her daughter as accomplice. The girl is demanded for punishment. The father defends her.

It would not profit you, girl, that your brother loved you, had not your mother hated him. The abominable woman, a stepmother even to her daughter, could not even die unless she also killed. Among gladiators too the lot of a victor who fights with a dying man is hard. You may fear no adversary more than one who cannot live, but can kill. Most furious is the frenzy in despair, and in the last death the mind is driven to madness. Some wild beasts bite the very weapons, and rush through their wounds upon the author of their death; the gladiator whom, armed, he had fled, naked he pursues; and men cast down headlong drag with them not only what pushed them, but what meets them. By a certain natural feeling of a mind given over to ruin, it is most pleasing to the dying to die together. O a lie like a poisoning! While she remembers the stepmother, she has forgotten the mother. I ask that, because I avenged my son, I may not lose my daughter. Unless you help me, the stepmother has won, I am conquered. Not even amid her tortures did she cease to kill. Let it profit the girl with you that her father praises her, let it profit her that her mother accuses her. "The daughter," she says, "is an accomplice." I began to be tortured, the stepmother to torture. I had such a son that a stepmother could love him, had she not fallen in with one who could hate even her own daughter. A slave, tortured for theft, named Cato as accomplice. Which do you believe more, the tortures or Cato? Why did the stepmother speak so late, the girl so soon? In this she was paying the penalty for poisoning, that she might exact the price of her accusation.

The other side. The cubs of certain wild beasts are born along with their fury; poisons are deadly at once in their roots. What of the woman who scattered her stepson to delay the father who followed? You have an example that fits both a sister and a maiden. The stepmother gave poison to this stepson, that her daughter alone might be heir; therefore she took an accomplice too.

The thief who accused of treason. A certain man, having accused a rich man of treason, by night pierced through his wall and carried off the chest in which letters sent by the enemy had been placed. The rich man was condemned. When the accuser wished to address the assembly, he was barred by the magistrate; he brings an action for injury.

I carried off only what a thief would have left. I feared nothing more, as a thief, than that the owner might be unwilling to acknowledge the theft. The ruin of one wall held up the falling state of the city. I declare my information: the city is privy to my theft. Is it a theft, when the owner fears to acknowledge it? When the man who lost it suffered punishment, and the man who carried it off a reward? To which would you rather have allowed to speak, if at the same time both the thief and the owner had come? You leaders of a thousand ships, you took Troy by theft. If cities are well overthrown by theft, how much better are they freed by it? I came into the forum, I told of my nocturnal expedition. All had assembled as though for a public meeting. Why do you remove me before the accusation, when not even traitors perish unheard? O the theft, worthy to be told in the assembly! The most vigilant breast of a traitor, ever busy for our destruction, the public destinies had lulled to sleep; sleep had so bound his ministers too, that I was free to choose what I should take. I seemed to myself to be tearing down the walls of the enemy. Do you call it a theft, than which nothing better was done in your year of office? No thief plots against the commonwealth. There is nothing that is not permitted on behalf of the commonwealth.

The other side. What a spectacle that was, you gods! The fortune of the commonwealth had matched together a thief and a traitor. When he saw his theft was useless, he betrayed it, to sell to you what he could sell to no one — so cunning a thief that he could impose even on a traitor. He wishes the bad luck of his theft to seem a plan. The law which bids a nocturnal thief be killed in any manner whatever speaks not only of a condemned man, but of a thief; it hates this vice, and not undeservedly: it is not far from a traitor. He carried off not what he chose, but what the destiny of the public good luck threw in his way. At one and the same time he showed us both a traitor and a thief, who would rather plunder a rich man than condemn him. He broke into the house with stealthy hand; he eluded him. This was not the first time he did it; but he carried off not what he wished, but what he could. By a good precedent the traitor was condemned, by a bad one he was found out.

The tyrannicide released by the pirates. Children are to support their parents, or else be imprisoned. A certain man killed one brother who was a tyrant and another caught in adultery, while their father pleaded for them. Captured by pirates, he wrote to his father about his ransom. The father sent a letter to the pirates: if they cut off the man's hands, he would pay double the money. The pirates released him. The father fell into poverty and asks for support. When the son refuses, the father wishes to have him led off to prison. The son speaks against it.

"If you cut them off" — if you are angry, write rather, "if you kill him." As a tyrannicide, I ask for the tyrant's end. I do not fear that the judges should bind the hands the pirates loosed. You plead for an adulterous son. Now ask how tyrants come to be made. "I will give double" — it is plain, he pleads for an only son. "I will give double" — one sum for the son, one for the tyrannicide. "If you cut off his hands" — this we did neither to the adulterer nor to the tyrant. And do you even now demand my hands? Deny that the letter is yours; and you have the proof — say: I am in the habit of pleading even for the adulterer. They sent me back to the commonwealth with my hands, to my father with his letters. This was wanting to the tales of our age — that the story should be told of a man loosed by pirates and bound by his father. A buyer of cruelty such as not even a pirate would be the seller. "I will give double" — what need of it? I could have been freed more cheaply. "That you cut off his hands" — the brigands were dumbfounded and said: tell your father that pirates do not sell everything. What kind of father to wish for I do not know: rich, he cripples me; poor, he binds me; neither course suits my hands. Where is the patrimony with which you equip tyrants, with which you make adulterers?

The other side. I have reared three monsters raging against each other and against me: one who could crush his country, another who could violate his brother, another his father. This law was written for bad fathers; for good ones are supported even without a law. I knew the pirates would not act unless they received money; and had they hoped for it, they would surely have cut off his hands. That was no anger of a father, but cunning: I had nothing from which to ransom him, I could beg of no one in a city so greedy that not even sons support their fathers; I used my judgement, knowing that pirates are not cruel but greedy: I made them despair of being able to ransom him. Whether I planned it wisely I do not know; for the moment I planned it luckily. My mind was driven out of me from the time I saw one son on the citadel, another in adultery, a third in parricide, while I was left alone, childless, an old man. This colour must be carried off by sheer force of feeling; for great power is needed to make oneself pitiable by self-accusation. I remember the man was called sane among scholars, and a scholar among the sane.

The foreign trader. A certain man who had a beautiful wife went abroad. A foreign trader moved into the woman's neighbourhood; three times he solicited her for sexual relations, raising his offers; she refused. The trader died; in his will he left the beautiful woman heir to all his goods, and added this notice: "because I found her chaste." She entered upon the inheritance. The husband returns and accuses her of adultery on suspicion.

Late is the complaint I bring: I do not accuse my wife of adultery until she is made rich. After such great profits of unchastity, if I can keep silent, I must confess that this was my reason for being away. It is time that a husband be believed concerning his wife. Let a married woman keep her eyes cast down to the ground, and toward an obliging caller be ungracious rather than immodest; let her refuse her unchastity by her looks far sooner than by her word. No one will ask again the woman who refuses with spirit. "Be sole heir of all my goods, because you could not be corrupted, because you so faithfully guarded your chastity." Pass over for a moment the name of the author: is it not the will of a husband that is believed? Has all the forbearance of our age now so departed that, against a husband's complaint, a wife is defended by another man's testimony? The foundation of women's vices is greed. She who can be without fear of the reputation of adultery, can be without fear of adultery. From every reef the purple-fish is gathered, with which the dress may be stained as with blood. Unhappy throngs of slave-girls labour, that the adulteress may be visible through a thin gown, and that a husband may know nothing more in his own wife's body than any stranger or foreigner. The old verdict I will assess by the future; meanwhile, what asks for her he found her — unchaste. All call you unchaste; chaste only one man, and a foreigner, who does more harm as praiser than as accuser. I never heard my wife called chaste except in the adulterer's notice. Cast your eyes to the ground and shut your ears to the voices of strangers: let each man refuse for himself on your behalf. He called her chaste, I call her unchaste: you will, I think, believe a citizen rather than a foreigner, a husband rather than an adulterer. The very notice he wrote with the mind of a seducer. "Because I found her chaste," he says — which befell no man but me.

The other side. She is beautiful: this was Nature's fault. She was without her husband: this was the husband's fault. She was solicited: this was another man's fault. She refused: this was chastely done. She was left an heir: this was good fortune. She entered upon the inheritance: this she did deliberately.

pr.1. I have known certain men, most eloquent, who did not answer to their reputation when they declaimed; speaking in the forum to the greatest admiration of all, the moment they withdrew to these domestic exercises they were deserted by their own talent. That this should happen to a good many is to me as strange as it is certain. And so I remember asking Cassius Severus what the reason was that in declamations his eloquence did not answer to him.

pr.2. For in no one did this happen more remarkably. His speech was vigorous, polished, full of mighty epigrams; no one allowed less of idleness in his pleading; there was no part that did not stand by its own merit, nothing in which a hearer could turn his mind elsewhere without loss, all of it intent, all aiming at some mark; no one held the feelings of his audience more in his own power. True is what our friend Gallio says of him: "When he spoke, he was master of the case, so completely did all do what he bade; when he wished it, they grew angry."

pr.3. "No one, while he spoke, but feared he would leave off." You must not judge him by what he published; there are indeed even these things by which his eloquence may be recognized; yet he was far greater heard than read. This did not happen to him in the proportion in which it happens to almost all to whom being heard is a greater recommendation than being read, but in him the difference is far greater. First, there was as much in the man as in the talent: a striking size of body, the sweetness of a most powerful voice — though these rarely come together, that the same voice be at once sweet and solid — a delivery such as could have produced an actor, and yet not such as could seem an actor's.

pr.4. For there was nothing you would wonder at in him more than that the gravity which was wanting to his life was overflowing in his pleading: so long as he kept himself short of jests, his speech was that of a censor. Then, the very things he spoke were better than what he wrote. For being a man of ready presence of mind, and of greater talent than application, he pleased more in the things he discovered than in the things he had brought prepared. And indeed when angry he spoke better, and so men took the most careful precaution not to interrupt him while speaking.

pr.5. He alone profited by being caught off guard; fortune always deserved better of him than care. Yet this good luck never persuaded him to negligence. In one day he would plead several private cases, and so as to plead one before noon, another after; but a public case never more than one in a day. And yet I do not know of any defendant he undertook except himself: so completely did he find nowhere any subject for speaking except in his own perils.

pr.6. He never spoke without notes, nor was he content with that kind of notes in which the bare facts are set down, but for the most part the pleading was written out in full; even those things that could be said wittily were jotted down; but though he would not come forward unless equipped, he gladly fell away from his apparatus. Forced to speak extempore, he outran himself beyond measure. It was always more useful for him to be caught out than to be prepared; but you would admire him the more for not abandoning his diligence, since rashness served him so well.

pr.7. He had, then, everything that might equip him to declaim well: a diction not common nor sordid, but choice; a manner of speaking not slack or languid, but ardent and impetuous; explanations not slow nor empty, but holding more of thought than of words; diligence, the greatest support even of a middling talent. Yet when he declaimed he was not only far below himself, but below many: and so he rarely declaimed, and not unless forced by friends.

pr.8. But when I asked why in declamations he was unequal to himself, he would say this: "What you wonder at in me happens to nearly all. Even great talents — from which I know I am far removed — when have they excelled in more than one work? Cicero's eloquence forsook him in his verses; that felicity of talent left Vergil in unfettered prose; Sallust's speeches are read for the honour of his histories; the speech of the most eloquent man, Plato, which was written for Socrates, is worthy neither of the advocate nor of the defendant.

pr.9. "This you may see happen not only to talents but to bodies, whose strengths are not suited to all that is done by strength: with this one no one is a match in wrestling; that one is mighty to lift a load of great weight; that one, whatever he grasps, does not let go, but lays his hands, that will hold them back, on vehicles thrusting downhill. I come to animals: some hounds are bred for the boar, some for the stag; the swiftness of horses, though they be very fast, is not fitted for the racecourse in all; some better endure a rider, some the yoke.

pr.10. "To call you to my own malady: Pylades in comedy, Bathyllus in tragedy, fell far short of themselves; to my namesake, since swiftness of foot is not only not conceded but cast in his teeth, the hands are slower; some fight best against the heavy-armed, some against the Thracians, and some so desire to be matched with a left-handed man as . . . In oratory itself, although the subject be one, yet he who argues best narrates more carelessly; that one does not fill out so well as he prepares. Our friend Passienus, when he begins to speak — straight after his exordium there is a general flight; for the epilogue we all return; only those who must, hear the middle parts.

pr.11. "Do you wonder that the same man does not declaim as well as he pleads cases, or that the same man does not speak deliberative themes so well as forensic ones? Pompeius Silo, seated, is both fluent and learned, and would be reckoned eloquent if he would dismiss us after his preface: he declaims so badly that I seem to have wished him well when I said, 'May you never rise.' A great and varied thing is eloquence, and it has not yet so indulged anyone as to fall to him whole; he is fortunate enough who has been admitted to some part of it.

pr.12. "I, however, seem able also to give my own reason: I have grown accustomed to look not at a hearer but at a judge; I have grown accustomed not to answer myself but my opponent; I avoid saying superfluous things no less than contradictory ones. In a school-piece what is not superfluous, when the thing itself is superfluous? I will show you my feeling: when I speak in the forum, I am doing something; when I declaim, it is, as Censorinus very prettily used to say of those who ambitiously sought offices in country towns: I seem to myself to be labouring in a dream. Then the very thing is different:

pr.13. "it is one thing entirely to fight, another to flourish weapons in the air. The school has always been so reckoned to be a kind of training-ground, the forum the arena; and that is why a man about to speak for the first time in the forum is called a raw recruit. Come now, lead those declaimers into the senate, into the forum: they will be changed along with the place; like bodies accustomed to a closed room and a pampering shade, they cannot stand in the open, they do not know how to bear rain or sun, they will scarcely find themselves; for they have grown used to being eloquent at their own pleasure.

pr.14. "You must not look for an orator in this boyish exercise. What if you should wish to judge a helmsman in a fish-pond? I would excuse myself to you more carefully, as if I were not born for this thing, did I not know that both Asinius Pollio and Messala Corvinus and Passienus, who now stands in the first rank, are less well received than Cestius or Latro.

pr.15. "Which, then, do you think is the fault — of those who speak or of those who hear? They do not speak worse, but these judge with worse taste, who, being mostly boys or youths, frequent the schools; these not only prefer their Cestius to the most eloquent men I mentioned a little while ago, but would prefer him even to Cicero, if they did not fear stones. Yet in the one way they can, they do prefer him: for they learn this man's declamations by heart, and read that man's speeches only those to which Cestius wrote replies.

pr.16. "I remember entering his school when he was about to recite his speech against Milo; Cestius, after his custom, said in self-admiration: 'If I were a Thracian, I would be Fusius; if I were a pantomime, I would be Bathyllus; if a horse, Melissio.' I could not contain my bile and cried out: 'If you were a sewer, you would be the Great Sewer.' Huge was the laughter of all; the schoolmen stared at me, asking who I was that had so thick a neck. Cestius, about to reply to Cicero, found nothing to answer me, but said he would not go on unless I left the house.

pr.17. "I said I would not leave a public bath until I had bathed. Then it pleased me to give Cestius satisfaction concerning Cicero in the forum. Catching him soon after, I summon him to law before the praetor, and when I had poured out as much jesting and abuse as I wished, I demanded that the praetor admit his name under the law concerning recorded wrongdoing. So great was his confusion that he asked for an adjournment. Then I brought him before another praetor and prosecuted him for ingratitude. Now before the city praetor I was asking that a guardian be appointed for him; when friends intervened — they had run together for this spectacle — and entreated me, I said I would trouble him no further if he would swear that Cicero was more eloquent than himself. And not by jest nor in earnest could he be brought to do this."

pr.18. "I have told you this little tale," he said, "that you might know that in declamations there is almost another race of men. If I wish to be compared with them, I need not a greater talent, but a smaller taste." And so it could scarcely now be obtained of him that he should declaim; and this could not be obtained at all — that he should be willing to have any hearers but his most intimate friends. And so he did. His declamations were unequal, but those passages that stood out, if you had set them in any declamation whatever, would have made it unequal: a rough arrangement, and one that avoided arrangement, but living epigrams. It will, however, be unfair to judge him by what I shall presently add; for these are not the things he said best, but the things I best remember.
Poison given to a frenzied son. A father gave poison to his son, who was frenzied and tearing his own limbs. He is accused by his wife of ill-treatment.
It is no wonder why she lives who has lost her son: he lives who killed him.
The other side. The one I was losing every day, I at last buried. You are mistaken, unhappy woman, as to the time of your bereavement: not then did you lose your son, but then you buried him.

Outside. Alfius Flavus spoke this epigram: "He was himself both his own nourishment and his own undoing." Cestius, rebuking him as though he had spoken with a corrupt taste, said: "It is plain that you read the poets eagerly: that thought is his who has filled this age not only with amatory arts but with amatory epigrams. For Ovid in his books of Metamorphoses says: 'He himself began to rend his own limbs with mangling bite, and the unhappy man fed his body by diminishing it.'"

The tyrannicide who was the tyrant's lover. Let there be a reward for a tyrannicide. A man caught in adultery by the tyrant wrested the sword from the tyrant and killed him. He seeks the reward. There is opposition.
