He would not have done the tyrannicide, had the tyrant not armed him. Whose lover was he not, who was even the tyrant's? He charges us with the fact that, caught in adultery, he was unwilling to die. Your tyrannicide might lawfully have been killed by the tyrant. A contest entered into on equal terms public fortune drew apart: not the more innocent conquered, but the stronger. The tyrant brought a sword with him; for so those come who mean to kill. Why do you alone come for the reward? You certainly killed the tyrant along with an adulteress. He took up no breastplate or shield, but a thin and transparent garment; drenched in perfume, he entered the chamber, in which he had carefully ascertained that the tyrant was not. Our tyrannicide prayed that he might not find the tyrant. Let the tyrant lead a tyrannicide to the citadel — not his wife; hatred, not love; when about to climb, let him bring a spirit, let him bring a blade; let him go where he may find the tyrant. Every honourable work the will begins, the opportunity completes. Virtue is often honoured even where the outcome has failed it; crimes too are punished, though they have stopped short of the outcome; an unlucky virtue does not lose the title of glory, nor does fortuitous good luck intercept the glory of virtue. Never would the wisdom of our ancestors buy a tyrannicide with such great gifts, if lust too could promise it. They fought in a new and unheard-of fashion, the tyrannicide for adultery, the tyrant for chastity. You killed a husband; fortune killed a tyrant. I wish a tyrant to fall for the commonwealth; let an angry citizen kill him, let him mingle with the wounds such curses as a husband would have brought against an adulterer. From an adulteress's kisses you run to a reward. I would not have a tyrannicide play the lover before he kills the tyrant. The Roman people would not have its enemy conquered by poison, nor by treachery. I will honour a sudden tyrannicide; I will not honour a fortuitous one, nor a forced one.

The other side. "You had no blade," he says. For what did it profit the tyrant that he had one? In the man who comes unarmed to a tyrant the valour is not less, but the danger greater. Do not ask what I brought into the citadel; I brought back a tyrannicide. The sword is not mine; but the hand is mine, the spirit is mine, the plan, the danger, the tyrannicide are mine. Do you call adultery the means by which it was brought about that no one fear adultery? The citadel being carefully fortified, seeking an opportunity, I tried the slaves, I tried the friends; through the wife alone the opportunity shone forth. I did not think that to defile the tyrant's wife was adultery, any more than to kill a tyrant is homicide. To carry a blade into the citadel was dangerous; to find one, easy. "If I find the tyrant," I said, "whatever lies to hand will be a weapon. Surely a tyrant is always wont to have a blade about him. The sword, between two men, belongs to the stronger." How anxious an adulterer I was, lest I should not be caught!

The men not received by the general. Let it not be lawful to open the gates by night in war. Let a general in war have supreme power. Three hundred men, taken captive by the enemy, came to the gates by night; the general did not open; before the gates they were killed. After the victory the general is made defendant for harming the commonwealth.

I did not think them my own men; they knew the law. "Why," he says, "did the three hundred perish?" Nay, why, that they might not perish, were they taken captive? These men I would not have received by day, unless as conquerors; by night, not even as conquerors. Going forth the next day into battle, I showed to men about to fight three hundred in whom nothing could be praised but flight, nothing missed but their number. They flee, to forsake the laws; they return, to abolish them. The Roman people, in the battle of Cannae, reduced to the utmost straits, when it longed for the help of slaves, despised that of captives, and believed that those could better guard liberty who had never had it than those who had lost it. By night, how am I to distinguish enemy and citizen? What mark do you give me, that I may recognize their arms? I believe the enemy were in ambush, to kill those shut out, and pursue those let in.

The other side. He was hostile to the three hundred; he had stationed them in an unfavourable place; that this might not be proved, he did not receive them. Most valiant generals have been taken captive — Regulus, Crassus. This was the last word of the men entreating: "Send us arms"; this at least the law does not forbid.

The madman who gave up his wife to his son. Let there be an action for madness. A man who had two sons married a wife. One of the young men, when he was ill and at the last, the physicians said had a sickness of the mind. The father entered to his son with drawn sword, and asked him to tell him the cause. He said he was in love with his stepmother. The father gave up his wife to him. He is accused by the other son of madness.

Hear a new thing: a cruel brother, a merciful stepmother. I am mad, because by my kindness someone is well. I handed over my wife to him; but I had snatched her away. "I call to witness," he said, "the gods who watch over filial love: I began to love her before you married her." So you call it an injury, that you have a brother and have not a stepmother? I passed before this man's eyes with a blade; no one but a sick man wrested the sword from me. To a father who could not endure the danger of a dying son, pardon must be given in whatever deed.

The other side. One was cured by pandering, the other recovered by parricide. What? Do you not think that adultery, which is committed with the husband bringing it about? I do not know whether he married more madly, or kept her, or dismissed her, or gave her away. How mad is the man to whom adultery is reckoned as a kindness! The husband drew his sword, not to avenge adultery, but to bring it about. The brother ought rather to have died than to be healed disgracefully. For what if he had coveted his mother, his sister? Some remedies are graver than the dangers themselves. Everything was contrived between stepson and stepmother; a sickness was feigned, and a father mocked by the basest of mimes.

Beware the traitor. A father and son sought the command; the son was preferred. When war was joined he was captured. Ten envoys were sent to ransom the general. As they went, the father met them; he said that he had brought the gold for the ransom too late, that his son had been crucified. They arrived, and the general said to them from the cross: "Beware the traitor." The father is made defendant for treason.

The general bore the punishment, the traitor the price. We saw this man sadder when his son was declared general than when he was captured. How did you return safe, an old man, alone, with the gold, when even generals are captured? He received more gold than could be hidden. Do not wonder: he had sold both the general and his son. "Beware the traitor." We have already taken care, at the elections. The enemy would have taken the gold from you, had they not given it. "Beware the traitor." The dying man's information was brief, the son's modest. Why were you let go? If nothing else, you both begot a leader and wished to be a leader yourself. He came forward as a candidate against his father: even then he modestly informed against us. Your son was unwilling to entrust the commonwealth to you. Our envoys carried gold, the father carried it off. You did not stand rigid and motionless, you did not cling there as if you too were fixed to it. Why do you withdraw so quickly? He still lives and speaks. By his voice he informed of the treason, by his silence of the traitor. The best of generals did not cease to care for the commonwealth even on the cross. To you he did not say: beware the treason. Neither could the general be silent about the treason, nor the son speak of the traitor. Wait while the envoys are sent. You say: feeling does not endure delay. Then if you cannot ransom him alive, at least ransom him dead. Never was an enemy so hard that he was not bent by a father's tears. "Beware the treason"; that is, let no one go out without the guards' knowledge, let no one reach the enemy without the commonwealth's knowledge, let no one return from the enemy's camp heavy with gold. Nothing is wanting to the information: of the treason the general tells you, of the traitor the envoys. The question is removed. Do you ask whom he meant? Look at the man to whom he said nothing.

The other side. At the elections I yielded to my son. I did not wait for the decree, but, frantic and astounded, I ran off at once. In short, I made haste and did not arrive in time. I knew that enemies are often bent by fathers' tears.

Outside. Latro did not trouble to say that no treason had been committed, but that he was not the traitor. "A man who defends more than himself," he said, "is suspect to the judge." Cestius, having set the deliberative theme — "Alexander deliberates whether to sail the Ocean, when a voice was heard: 'How far, O unconquered one?'" — to a pupil who was describing at length Alexander's victories and the nations subdued, and adding, "how far after these?" cried out: "And you, how far?"

The thrice-brave man. Whoever has done a brave deed three times shall be exempt from military service. A father holds back his thrice-brave son, who wishes to go out into the battle line a fourth time; when the son refuses, he disowns him.

What is left over from my country I claim for myself, the father. O how weary I am already, with my son still fighting! Now on your behalf I cannot tell what even the law fears. Do you wonder if what is enough for the law is too much for a father? My reason for disowning is that I may not live without a son. My power to disown is in the power of the disowned. The best end of valour is to leave off before you fail. The law too, in the thrice-brave man, either distrusts him or takes thought for him.

The other side. Surely the disowned are allowed to fight. It shames me — the thrice-conquered serve in the army. A senator, after his sixty-fifth year, is neither compelled nor forbidden to come into the senate-house. Whatever is given in the name of honour is permitted either way; otherwise it ceases to be a reward, if necessity is laid upon it. You command leisure to a spirit that is not at leisure. A tumult has broken out; the eyes of all the citizens are turned upon me, and as yet, the truth must be told, my country owes me nothing: I have never fought except under compulsion. So far my soldiering has been the law's duty. The Athenians won the day with a disowned man for their general. What a difference! He blotted out his disowning by his valour; I earned mine.

The Olynthian father charged with assembling a mob. Let one who has made a gathering and an assembly be liable to capital punishment. When Olynthus was conquered, an old Olynthian came with his young son to Athens. The Athenians decreed citizenship to all the Olynthians. Invited to dinner by a dissolute young man, he came with his son. There, when there was mention of debauching the son, the father fled, and the young man was held back. The father began to weep before the house; the house was set on fire; ten young men perished, and the Olynthian's son. The father is accused of having made a gathering and an assembly.

If a wretched man is not allowed to weep, he must weep the more. Silence cannot be commanded to grief. There were men among the people who said: "Here he debauched my son, here my wife"; each man brought there both his own fire and his own grief. I fear, my son, that while I seek you I may fall upon the bones of some ravisher. Where is the good faith of Athens? Where are the hospitable hands joined on either side? "We are taken captive, my son," I said; "while we may, let us flee — but as from Philip. At least in Philip's hands we were men together." My tears are turned into a charge, as though from the time Olynthus was taken I had ceased to weep. So great, forsooth, am I, that I could rouse the people in a city in which I could not save my son. It is not, whenever several have come together to some place, a gathering and an assembly, but whenever men have been called together, whenever, prepared as if to their leader, they have run together; not if one neighbourhood has met, or the number of a few passers-by has flowed in, but where the whole people, or the greater part of it, where the city has been divided into parties. A gathering is the name for a great multitude coming together by some common agreement: but there at the start there were few, and then the rest came together not to me, but to the fire — which, even so, the people chose to watch rather than put out. The law punishes not the man on whose account a gathering was made, but the man by whom it was made. Vengeance was not so dear to me that I should be willing to lose my son; and I tried to beg the people, and could not.
The other side. What need of a gathering? There are laws written for the avenging of all wrongs. Once stirred, a multitude keeps no measure. The city might have burned in that fire.

The patron reclaiming the services he had remitted. Let things done by force and fear be void. In the civil war a patron, conquered and proscribed, took refuge with his freedman. He was received by him and asked to remit his services. He remitted them, a formal record being made. Restored, he imposes the services. The freedman speaks against it.

As patron I seek restoration from my freedman. If you had wished then to bargain with me for the services, I would have given my word. I lost my goods in the war; I came to my restoration stripped bare; now I look to the services of my freedmen. Bring out the tablets, crueller than that tablet of proscription: that one pursued those it had conquered, these pursued those they had received; in that one was vengeance, in these treachery; in short, that one has now ceased, these persist. "It was not my force," he says, "but another's." He is equally deserving of punishment who himself applies force and who uses to his own profit the force applied by another. I fell first upon this man, and while I feared to offend, I followed him in his demand. He did not receive me, he shut me in. Nothing is baser than a venal mercy.

The other side. You have no need of power: you know that he obeys you even when he cannot be compelled. Whatever services you impose, you will never impose any so dangerous as those you imposed. I have your own judgements: you judged well of a slave — you freed him; well of a freedman — proscribed, you entrusted yourself to me of all men. If I had not wished to have a patron, I could have done so. You were the one of the proscribed who could then even be entreated. Your restoration remitted to you your proscription; it did not annul whatever you did during the proscription.

Outside. All inveighed against the freedman. Varius Geminus and Otho Junius pleaded more gently, so that the patron should seem about to remit the services, if he won. For Otho said: "Let me seem by my own judgement to have remitted them; I will do it, I will remit them. Why do you fear me as though I had promised against my will?" On the contrary Cestius says: colours of this kind are to be used then, when there is reason to fear that we may seem to demand a hard thing, when, against an honourable person, the judge must be beguiled by a gentler promise. What do we fear in this person and cause, except this one thing that must be feared from this colour — that, if we wish to remit it, we may even seem to have wished to?

The tyrant a candidate after an amnesty. Let it be lawful for a candidate to speak against a candidate. A tyrant laid down his despotism under an amnesty, so that if anyone reproached him with the tyranny, he should be punished with death. He seeks a magistracy; a rival candidate speaks against it.

As a candidate I pledge, in my year, no woman shall be carried off, no man killed, no temple plundered. Let him tell why for so long he has held no offices — I beg it by our common liberty. I shall die; it will be cast in your teeth that you killed a citizen. He wishes to be distinguished by some command, some power — a man of great nobility, great influence, vast wealth. There is said to have been a master of Sicily who shut men in bronze bulls and burned them with fires set beneath, so that they uttered a bellowing and could not utter words. O a man fastidious in his very cruelty, who, though he wished to torture, yet was unwilling to hear!

The other side. Whatever I did, whatever I carried out, I did for the sake of the commonwealth. I ask that the law passed for me do me no harm, nor that anything harm me because that is not charged which, if charged, would do no harm.

The verse of the Vestal Virgin. A Vestal Virgin wrote this verse: "Happy the wedded! May I die if marriage is not sweet." She is charged with unchastity. "Happy the wedded" — this is the word of one who longs for it; "may I perish if" — this is the word of one who affirms; "marriage is sweet" — either you swear from experience or you forswear from inexperience; neither befits a priestess. To you the magistrates lower their fasces, to you the consuls and praetors yield the road; are you a virgin for so paltry a reward? Let a priestess swear rarely, and never except by her own Vesta. "May I die" — has the eternal fire been put out? "May I die" — have you been approached about marriage? You at last, Vesta, I invoke, that you be as hostile to your priestess as you are hateful to her. Recite the verse, while I ask what kind it is. Would you write verse, would you soften words to your own measures, and break by melody the severity owed to the temple? But if you must needs praise marriage, tell of Lucretia, write of her death before you swear about your own. O you, worthy of every punishment, to whom anything is happier than the priesthood! "It is sweet" — how vivid a word, how sent up from the depths of the heart, not only of one who has experienced it but of one who has delighted in it. Even without defilement, she who longs for defilement is unchaste.

The other side. One verse is charged against her, and not even this one whole. "She ought not," he says, "to write verse." It is a great difference whether you rebuke or punish. No one can be condemned for unchastity but a woman whose body has been violated. What? Do you think that poets write what they feel? She lived modestly, with restraint; her dress was not too luxurious, her converse with men not too free; I confess to you her one crime: she has talent. Why should she not envy Cornelia? Why not the woman who bore Cato?
Outside. Varius Geminus said before Caesar: "Caesar, those who dare to speak before you are ignorant of your greatness; those who do not dare, of your humanity."

The choice to be changed when the ravisher is convicted. Let a ravished woman choose either the death of her ravisher or marriage without a dowry. A ravished woman, brought forward, chose marriage. The young man denied that he was the ravisher. He was convicted. She seeks his death. The ravisher speaks against it.

It was lawful for you to choose no more than once. Set before yourselves the face of punishment, the executioner, the axe: that this be lawful even once is too much. In this confusion I was so led astray that I did not know what I had done. I am punished more heavily when I am ashamed of having sinned than when I sinned. She chose marriage; and she did not yet know how modest a husband she would have. You let the ravisher go; will you kill the husband? Is then what he violated less than what he denied? So did we deny the wrong more dangerously than we did it? On a certain night — what shall I say? It is no longer a shame not to deny. Night, wine, error — why are you angry, girl? Now he does not deny it. A judge cannot recall the tablet he has cast concerning a defendant; the examiner does not change his pronouncement. Nothing is so civil, so useful, as that a power that is great should be brief. If you choose death today, you will do what has never been done: you will have chosen both.

The other side. In the former trial his aim was to pay no penalty at all for the defilement; in this his aim is that he himself should make the choice. Would that what frees him from fear — that he knows the clemency of his own judge — did not do so. There is a certain modesty close to innocence, to offer oneself to the laws. The law does not add how often she may choose, but from what: "either this," it says, "or that"; it does not add: "not more than once."

The crucifixion of the slave who refused his master poison. A master, being ill, asked his slave to give him poison. He did not give it. He provided in his will that the slave be crucified by the heirs. The slave appeals to the tribunes.

Cornelian law, I call upon you; behold, my master commands what you forbid. That no one may think he had displeased his master, he ordered the cross prepared for him at the same time as the poison for himself. We confess more crimes of the slave: he refused his master, when he wanted them, untimely draughts and harmful foods. For what did he not want, who asked for poison? He chose to suffer the cross rather than to deserve it. If he loses, he is to die; if he does not lose, he is to be the slave of the man by whom he is demanded for the cross. On one side is the law, on the other the will, and on both sides the cross. The madman wanted to kill his slave without cause. Do you seek a proof of his madness? He wanted to kill himself too. "The tribunes," he says, "cannot help a slave." A slave's son we had for a king; by a slave's information the conspiracy of Brutus's sons with the Tarquins was laid bare. Is there, then, no difference whether a man gave his master poison or refused it? Even where to die is a remedy, to kill is a crime. Do you wish a slave to despair of his master's life as quickly as an heir does? If you think death a punishment, why do you ask for it? If a benefit, why do you threaten it? Does anyone reproach a man with poison except given poison? Will you set any limit to the tribunician power, which the Roman people, that it might itself have the most power, willed to be stronger than itself? To have poison is a crime as great as to kill one's master.

The other side. Wishing to die, he chose for this service the most worthless slave, a bold one, one hostile to him. He took thought not for his master's safety, whom he saw wasting away with an incurable disease, but prolonged his torments. A slave is not the censor of his master's command, but its minister. The right of wills is at stake, all the power of which has perished, if slaves disregard the commands of the living and become tribunes of the dead. So then, you gallows-bird, you will not die at your master's pleasure, but your master will die at yours?

pr.1. What the givers of games are wont to do, who, to keep the people's expectation in suspense, deal out new pairs of gladiators throughout all the days, so that there may be something both to delight the people and to recall it — this I do: I do not bring forth all at once; let the little book always have something new, so that it may stir you not only by the novelty of the epigrams, but also of their authors. Keener is the desire of learning the unknown than of going over the known. This we see happen in actors, in gladiators, in orators of whom fame has just promised something, in all things, in short:

pr.2. men flock to what is new, and do not come to what is known. Yet I will not wear out your expectation by bringing the men forth one by one: today I will be liberal and deal with a full hand. Asinius Pollio never declaimed with a crowd admitted; nor did ambition fail him in his studies: for he was the first of all Romans to recite his own writings before invited men. And from this comes what Labienus — a man of bitterer mind than tongue — says: "That old man of triumphs never committed his recitations to the people"; whether because he had too little confidence in them, or — what I should rather believe — so great an orator counted that work beneath his talent, and wished indeed to be exercised by it, but disdained to glory in it.

pr.3. I heard him both in his vigour and afterwards when he was an old man, when he was, as it were, instructing his grandson Marcellus Aeserninus. He would listen to him speaking, and first dispute about the part that Marcellus had spoken: he would point out what was passed over, fill out what was lightly touched, convict what was faulty. Then he would speak the opposite side. He was somewhat more florid in declaiming than in pleading: that strict, harsh, and over-angry judgement of his own talent so far stood idle that in many things he needed an indulgence which could scarcely be obtained from him.

pr.4. Marcellus, though a boy, was already of such promise that Pollio believed the succession of his own eloquence belonged to him, although he was leaving a son, Asinius Gallus, a great orator — but for this, that, as always happens, the greatness of his father did not bring him forward but buried him. I remember that, within the fourth day after he had lost his son Herius, he declaimed for us, but so much more vehemently than ever, that it was plain a man stubborn by nature was wrangling with his own fortune;

pr.5. nor did he relax anything from the accustomed order of his life. And so, when Gaius Caesar had died in Syria, and the deified Augustus complained by a letter — as was the way of that most merciful man, not only courteously but even familiarly — that in so great and recent a grief of his own a man most dear to him had dined at a full banquet, Pollio wrote back: "I dined on the very day I lost my son Herius." Who would exact a greater grief from a friend than from a father?

pr.6. O great men, who know not how to succumb to fortune, and make their adversities trials of their virtue! Asinius Pollio declaimed within the fourth day after he had lost his son: that proclamation was the act of a mighty spirit insulting its own ills. But on the other hand I know that Quintus Haterius bore the death of his son Sextus with so weak a spirit that not only did he yield to the recent grief, but could not endure even the memory of the old and faded one. I remember, when he was speaking the controversia about the man who, dragged away from the tombs of his three children, sues for injuries, his speech was broken in the middle by his weeping; then he spoke with so much the greater force, so much the more piteously, that it was plain how great a part of one's talent grief may sometimes be.

pr.7. Haterius declaimed extempore with the people admitted: he alone of all Romans whom I myself have known transferred the Greek facility into the Latin tongue. So great was the speed of his speech that it became a fault. And so the deified Augustus said very well: "Our Haterius needs a brake." So far did he seem not to run but to run downhill. Nor had he merely an abundance of words, but of matter too: as often as you wished, and as long as you wished, he would speak on the same theme, so many times over with new figures, new treatments, that he could be governed and not exhausted.

pr.8. By himself, however, he could not be governed; but he had a freedman whom he obeyed; he went just as that man either spurred him on or reined him in. He would bid him pass on when he had dwelt on a topic for some time: he passed on; he would bid him stand fast at the same topic: he stayed; he would bid him speak the epilogue: he spoke it. He had his talent in his own power, the measure of it in another's.

pr.9. He thought that to divide the controversia was to the purpose if one were questioning him, but not if one were hearing him. His order was the one that impulse had given; he did not direct himself to the declamatory rule. Nor did he guard his words. For the schools now shun certain words as if obscene, and cannot endure any that are somewhat coarse or drawn from everyday use. He, in this, humoured the schoolmen, that he should not use trodden and worn-out words; but he spoke certain old words, used by Cicero and then abandoned by the rest, which not even that most rapid current of his speech could hide. So far is anything unusual notable even in a crowd.

pr.10. This excepted, no one was either fitter for the schoolmen or more like them; but while he would speak nothing except elegantly, except brilliantly, he often fell into things that could not escape ridicule. I remember that, when he was defending a freedman charged with having been his patron's catamite, he said: "Unchastity in a free-born man is a crime, in a slave a necessity, in a freedman a duty." The thing went off into jests: "You do me no duty," and "He is much engaged in duties to that man." From this, the unchaste and the obscene were for a while commonly called "dutiful."

pr.11. I remember too that this rejoinder, set down by him thus, furnished great matter for the jests of Asinius Pollio and then of Cassius Severus: "But," he said, "amid the boyish bosoms of your schoolfellows you bade lust with an obscene hand." And very many things of this kind were charged against him. There was much you would reprehend, much you would admire, since he flowed like a torrent, great indeed but turbid. Yet he redeemed his faults with virtues, and had more for you to praise than to forgive — as in the declamation in which he wept.
